terms.gloss: The 'great schemer', the novel's con-man protagonist; narrator calls him Остап, others Бендер
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Ostap Bender, not Ostap Bendera/Ostapp); zh/ja spellings vary widely across existing editions

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of nobility; narrator uses name-and-patronymic throughout
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must be kept as the narrator's formal-comic register, not replaced with a surname or first name; ja/zh need a stable transcription of the awkward patronymic

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the priest who competes for the chairs
terms.why_hard: 'отец' is a clerical title (Father), not 'father' as kin; ja needs 神父 not 父

terms.gloss: Bender's recurring self-description: son of a Turkish subject (Odessa Jews often held Ottoman papers)
terms.why_hard: Formulaic epithet used by narrator repeatedly; must be rendered identically each time and 'подданный' is 'subject', not 'citizen' or 'Turk'

proposed.en: the son of a Turkish subject

terms.gloss: Konrad Karlovich Michelson, the false identity Bender assigns Vorobyaninov (from a stolen union card)
terms.why_hard: Reader must recognise it as an alias, not a new character; pair consistently with гражданин Михельсон

proposed.ja: コンラート・カルロヴィチ

terms.gloss: Same alias, surname form with the Soviet address 'citizen'
terms.why_hard: 'гражданин' is the ironic official Soviet address, not 'Mr'; keep one rendering of 'citizen' book-wide

terms.gloss: The late husband of the widow who owns a chair; Bender's ironic target
terms.why_hard: Surname must match вдова/мадам Грицацуева in feminine form; do not render as two different families

proposed.ja: グリツァツーエフ市民

terms.term: вдова Грицацуева / мадам Грицацуева / госпожа Грицацуева
terms.gloss: Madame Gritsatsuyeva, the widow Bender decides to marry; the chapter's 'sultry woman'
terms.why_hard: Three address forms (widow/madame/Mrs) shift register from official to mock-genteel; keep each distinct but the surname identical

proposed.en: the widow Gritsatsuyeva / Madame Gritsatsuyeva / Mrs Gritsatsuyeva
proposed.zh: 寡妇格里察楚耶娃 / 格里察楚耶娃夫人 / 格里察楚耶娃太太
proposed.ja: 未亡人グリツァツーエワ / マダム・グリツァツーエワ / グリツァツーエワ夫人

terms.gloss: Soviet official category: disabled veteran of the 'imperialist' (First World) war, entitled to benefits
terms.why_hard: Literal 'invalid of the imperialist war' is opaque; reader needs 'WWI disabled veteran' plus the Soviet label flavour

proposed.en: disabled veteran of the Imperialist War
proposed.zh: 帝国主义战争残废军人
proposed.ja: 帝国主義戦争の傷痍軍人

terms.gloss: Bender's joke: 'let's work like Marxists' — leave heaven to the birds, turn to material chairs
terms.why_hard: Parody of Soviet slogan-speak; must sound like a slogan, and the sky/birds line echoes Heine's 'Den Himmel überlassen wir den Engeln und den Spatzen'

proposed.en: let's proceed in a Marxist spirit
proposed.zh: 咱们按马克思主义的方法来办
proposed.ja: マルクス主義的にやろう

terms.gloss: Bender's mock-diplomatic label for his shipboard-style showdown with Father Fyodor in the corridor
terms.why_hard: Parodies newspaper reports of summit meetings; a flat rendering loses the mock-solemn diplomatic tone

proposed.en: today's ministerial meeting on the yacht
proposed.ja: 本日のヨット上での閣僚会談

terms.gloss: Marshal of the nobility, elected pre-revolutionary head of a district's gentry; Vorobyaninov's old office
terms.why_hard: Standard English is 'marshal of the nobility', not 'leader'; zh/ja need a fixed term, and Bender uses it as a taunt

terms.gloss: Bender's mock-Soviet nickname for Vorobyaninov ('chairman'), punning on his gentry title
terms.why_hard: Must be the same word as any real chairman elsewhere in the book so the pun on 'chair' survives; do not upgrade to 'president'

terms.gloss: Bender's running term for the chair hunt, borrowed from NEP-era foreign 'concessions'
terms.why_hard: Not a discount; render as the NEP economic term 'concession' every time so the running joke holds

terms.gloss: 'Gentlemen of the jury' — Bender's catchphrase, mock-courtroom rhetoric from the abolished tsarial jury system
terms.why_hard: Recurs book-wide; 'господа' is the pre-revolutionary address, ironic in 1927; keep one wording

terms.gloss: 'The hussar-monk', Bulanov, hero of Bender's inset story: a Petersburg cavalry officer who took the strictest monastic vows (схима)
terms.why_hard: схимник is a specific Orthodox rank (great schema), not simply 'hermit'; the comic collision hussar/ascetic must survive

terms.gloss: Count Alexei Bulanov, the hussar-monk of the inset story (based on Alexander Bulatovich)
terms.why_hard: Keep surname stable through the inset chapter; possible note on the real prototype

terms.gloss: The unnamed provincial town (Stargorod) of the opening chapters, in the Gogolian 'town of N' convention
terms.why_hard: Literary convention, not an abbreviation; keep the Latin 'N' in all languages

terms.gloss: Proverb: 'only cats are born quickly' — haste is for cats; a Bender line that became proverbial
terms.why_hard: Needs a punchy equivalent, not a literal calque that reads as nonsense; the same line recurs

proposed.en: Only cats are born in a hurry
proposed.ja: 早いのは猫の出産だけだ

terms.gloss: Odessa/Moscow slang for cheap showing-off, dandyish vulgarity; here 'robbing a widow is sheer pizhonstvo'
terms.why_hard: Not 'foppery' in the English sense; means crude bad form, amateurish show

terms.gloss: NEP-era shop-sign phrase 'chic moderne', Bender's approving verdict on his new shoes
terms.why_hard: Faux-French advertising cliché; should read as a borrowed label, not translated into plain 'stylish'

terms.gloss: Three words for the same pair of raspberry-coloured shoes in one scene (boots/shoes/dear little boots)
terms.why_hard: Translator must not invent three kinds of footwear; vary tone (diminutive) not object

proposed.zh: 皮鞋 / 鞋 / 这双小皮鞋
proposed.ja: 靴 / 短靴 / この靴ちゃん

terms.gloss: Post-1917 requisition of private property by Soviet authorities
terms.why_hard: Keep the administrative term 'requisitioned', not 'stolen' or 'taken'

terms.gloss: Plekhanov Street, a typical Soviet street renaming after the Marxist theorist
terms.why_hard: Transliterate as street name; do not translate Plekhanov

conventions: Soviet address 'гражданин/гражданка' is always 'Citizen' (公民 / 市民), never Mr/Mrs; 'господин/госпожа/мадам' keep their genteel or ironic flavour as Mr/Mrs/Madame.
Russian dialogue dashes become English quotation marks, zh 「」or “”, ja 「」; narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the same sentence, not footnoted.
Bender's recurring catchphrases (гражданин, господа присяжные заседатели, концессия, сын турецкого подданного) are bound once and repeated verbatim in all three languages.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the 'great schemer', young con man and co-hunter of the chairs; the narrator calls him by first name only
terms.why_hard: Spelling must be fixed once (Ostap, not Ostup/Ostapp) and the narrator's bare first name kept, unlike the full name-and-patronymic used for Vorobyaninov

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk; the narrator and other characters address him by name and patronymic
terms.why_hard: Name-plus-patronymic is the respectful form; dropping the patronymic or swapping in 'Mr Vorobyaninov' loses the pre-revolutionary deference Polesov shows him

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: surname of Ippolit Matveyevich; used by the narrator when he is acting rather than being addressed
terms.why_hard: One transliteration must be bound (Vorobyaninov) and kept distinct from the patronymic form so the reader sees both refer to the same man

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, a hopeless amateur mechanic and gossip of Stargorod, the 'intellectual locksmith'
terms.why_hard: Appears as Полесов, Виктор Михайлович, and слесарь-интеллигент on one page; all three must map to one character

terms.gloss: Polesov's name and patronymic, used by the narrator in mock-formal style
terms.why_hard: Must be tied to Polesov; the ceremonious full name is part of the joke about a fussy nobody

proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, fortune-teller, Vorobyaninov's old flame from before the revolution
terms.why_hard: Referred to only by name and patronymic here and by 'гадалка' at the end of the page; the two must read as the same woman

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: the narrator's recurring epithet for Polesov: a metal-fitter/mechanic with intellectual pretensions, a comic hybrid of two Soviet social categories
terms.why_hard: 'слесарь' is a fitter/mechanic, not a 'locksmith' in the modern sense; the hyphenated epithet must be one fixed phrase every time it recurs

terms.gloss: коммунальное хозяйство, the municipal communal-services department where Vorobyaninov met Polesov
terms.why_hard: A 1920s acronym meaningless to the target reader; must be rendered as a plain institution name, and the same rendering reused wherever it recurs

terms.gloss: pre-revolutionary polite formula 'I have not the honour [of knowing you]', which Vorobyaninov mumbles out of old habit
terms.why_hard: A literal 'I don't have the honour' sounds odd; it should read as a stiff, old-fashioned gentleman's rebuff, and the same formula recurs for him

terms.gloss: fortune-teller; Elena Stanislavovna's trade in NEP-era Stargorod, and the narrator's tag for her
terms.why_hard: Should be neutral 'fortune-teller', not 'witch' or 'psychic'; ja/zh need a female form consistent with later chapters

terms.gloss: Pereleshinsky Lane, the Stargorod side street where the fortune-teller lives
terms.why_hard: Fictional street; transliterate once and keep 'переулок' as Lane consistently across the book's many street names

terms.gloss: the narrator's mock-business label for Ostap and Vorobyaninov as partners in the chair hunt; alternates with концессионеры elsewhere
terms.why_hard: Must be kept distinct from концессионеры ('the concessionaires') and rendered the same each time so the running business-parody joke is visible

terms.gloss: 'mysterious stranger', Ostap's mock-romantic tag for Polesov, parodying adventure-novel cliche
terms.why_hard: Should sound like a pulp-novel cliche in each language, not a neutral description

terms.gloss: coarse verb 'to eat' (to stuff oneself); Ostap says 'безумно хочу жрать'
terms.why_hard: A polite 'I'd like some supper' kills Ostap's vulgar energy; needs a low-register but not obscene equivalent

proposed.zh: 我饿得要命，想大吃一顿

terms.gloss: through the connecting inner courtyards of old Russian towns, used as shortcuts and to avoid streets
terms.why_hard: The target reader may not know a courtyard can be a passage; the rendering must convey furtive shortcuts, not 'yards'

proposed.ja: 通り抜けの中庭を伝って

terms.gloss: chapter 13 title, one of Ostap's catchphrases (doctor's reassurance turned into mockery), later proverbial in Russian
terms.why_hard: It is a quotation-like tag that recurs in Ostap's mouth; the chapter title and the line in dialogue must match word for word

proposed.ja: 深呼吸を――あなたは興奮している！

terms.gloss: Ostap's characteristic gesture of thrusting his right shoulder forward before confronting someone
terms.why_hard: A recurring physical tag; translate the same way each time so the reader recognises Ostap's 'move'

proposed.ja: 右肩をぐいと前に出し

conventions: Personal names: transliterate once and bind (en BGN-style without diacritics, zh standard 新华社 transliteration, ja katakana with ・); keep Russian name-and-patronymic address as is, never replace with Mr/先生/さん.
Dialogue: Russian em-dash dialogue becomes quoted speech in each target (en “…”, zh “…”, ja 「…」); вы renders as ja です/ます and zh 您, ты as ja plain form and zh 你.
Soviet acronyms (комхоз, etc.): render as a short plain-language institution name in every language, identical throughout the book; no footnote unless the joke depends on the acronym itself.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The young con man, co-protagonist; Ostap Bender.
terms.why_hard: Spelling must be fixed once across all three scripts; the surname is stressed BEN-der, not Ben-DER, which matters for katakana.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility; the narrator alternates name-and-patronymic with the surname.
terms.why_hard: The alternation between 'Ипполит Матвеевич' and 'Воробьянинов' must be preserved, not collapsed to one form; patronymic transliteration must be stable.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇（沃罗比亚尼诺夫）
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ（ヴォロビャーニノフ）

terms.gloss: The narrator's recurring epithet for Bender: the great schemer/operator.
terms.why_hard: 'Combinator' is a false friend; the phrase is a book-wide brand and later became proverbial, so it needs one memorable rendering used every time.

terms.gloss: The narrator's mock-commercial epithet for the pair, from Ostap calling their treasure hunt a 'концессия' (a NEP-era state-granted business concession).
terms.why_hard: It is a running joke on NEP foreign-concession jargon, not a neutral word for 'partners'; it alternates with 'компаньоны' and both must stay distinct and consistent.

terms.gloss: The other recurring epithet for the pair: business partners.
terms.why_hard: Must be kept distinct from 'концессионеры'; 'companions' is wrong, the word is commercial.

terms.gloss: The yard-keeper's lodge where Tikhon lives, in the ground floor of Vorobyaninov's former house.
terms.why_hard: A дворник is a yard-keeper/janitor, not a doorman or porter; the lodge is a room, not a shed.

terms.gloss: The old yard-keeper of Vorobyaninov's former house, who still calls him 'барин'.
terms.why_hard: Name must be transliterated consistently; his speech is servile and pre-revolutionary and should stay so.

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary word for the master/gentleman of the house, used by servants; Tikhon's habitual word for Vorobyaninov.
terms.why_hard: It is deliberately anachronistic in 1927; render with an old-regime servant's word, not 'boss' or 'gentleman'.

terms.gloss: Russian felt boots; here the source of the manure smell in the lodge.
terms.why_hard: Not 'galoshes' or 'boots'; the whole joke depends on felt absorbing smells.

terms.gloss: Ostap parodies the chairman's formula closing a Soviet club 'evening of reminiscences'.
terms.why_hard: The comedy is the meeting-minutes register; it must sound like an official closing a session, not a casual 'enough nostalgia'.

proposed.en: I declare this evening of reminiscences closed
proposed.zh: 我宣布回忆晚会到此结束
proposed.ja: 本日の思い出の夕べは、これにて閉会とします

terms.gloss: The obsolete deferential particle -с (from 'сударь'), used by Ostap in mock-servile politeness.
terms.why_hard: Dropping it loses the mockery; over-translating gives Ostap a butler's voice. Needs one light book-wide device.

terms.gloss: To register one's residence with the local police (the Soviet propiska), required of hotel guests.
terms.why_hard: Not 'check in': it is police registration under one's passport name, which is exactly why Vorobyaninov fears it.

terms.gloss: The stolen identity Vorobyaninov adopts: a 48-year-old bachelor union member whose union card Ostap produces.
terms.why_hard: The alias recurs; the German-Baltic flavour of the name is part of the joke and must match how Vorobyaninov mishears it as a pre-revolutionary Senator Mikhelson.

proposed.zh: 康拉德·卡尔洛维奇·米赫尔松
proposed.ja: コンラート・カルロヴィチ・ミヘリソン

terms.gloss: Soviet trade union of employees in Soviet commerce (Союз советских торговых служащих), a real 1920s union.
terms.why_hard: A compressed Soviet acronym; the target reader needs it expanded once, and the contrast Senator vs. shop-clerk union member is the punchline.

proposed.en: the Union of Soviet Trade Employees
proposed.ja: ソヴィエト商業職員組合

terms.gloss: Literally 'ladybird'; colloquially a meek, harmless simpleton.
terms.why_hard: A literal 'ladybird' is meaningless; the target needs a 'meek creature' idiom of similar mildness.

proposed.ja: お人好しはやめなさい

terms.gloss: Trade-union membership booklet, which in the 1920s doubled as an identity document.
terms.why_hard: Reader must understand that this card can pass as ID at a hotel; 'union card' alone may not convey that.

terms.gloss: Not a member of the Communist Party, a standard line on Soviet forms.
terms.why_hard: Not 'independent' or 'non-partisan'; it is a formal personnel-file category.

terms.gloss: The Soviet civil police.
terms.why_hard: 'Militia' in English suggests an armed volunteer force; render as the police throughout.

terms.gloss: A children's game ('Rat') Ostap invokes as the model of innocence, contrasted with the Criminal Code.
terms.why_hard: The game is obscure even to Russians; the translator must decide whether to name it literally or substitute a familiar harmless game.

proposed.zh: 小孩子玩的捉老鼠游戏

terms.gloss: Two invented comic surnames: a florid Odessa-Greek one and one built on 'зловоние' (stench).
terms.why_hard: Zlovunov's meaning is the joke; a pure transliteration kills it, so the stench must be audible in the target name.

proposed.zh: 帕帕-赫里斯托佐普洛或者臭乌诺夫
proposed.ja: パパ・フリストゾプーロか、悪臭ノフ

terms.gloss: The provincial furnished-rooms hotel in Stargorod, grandly named after the Paris university.
terms.why_hard: 'Furnished rooms' was a class of cheap lodging below a hotel; keep the pretentious name untranslated and the category humble.

proposed.ja: 貸間ホテル「ソルボンヌ」

terms.gloss: The hotel floor attendant who services the rooms on a corridor.
terms.why_hard: Not 'bellboy' or 'porter'; he is the room servant of a cheap hotel and speaks with sly peasant deference.

terms.gloss: A provincial (guberniya-level) congress of delegates, whose visits prompt a hotel clean-up.
terms.why_hard: 'Губерния' still existed in 1927; render as 'provincial' consistently, not 'regional' or 'state'.

terms.gloss: Stargorod Communal Services Department (Старгородский коммунальный отдел/хозяйство), the municipal utilities and property office holding the old housing archive.
terms.why_hard: A Soviet portmanteau acronym; expand once, then keep the transliterated acronym since the narrator uses it as a name.

proposed.zh: 旧城公用事业局（斯塔尔科姆霍兹）
proposed.ja: スタルコムホーズ（スタルゴロド市公共事業局）

terms.gloss: The housing department that handled requisitioned property after 1917, disbanded in 1921.
terms.why_hard: Another acronym; must pair with Старкомхоз in the same style of rendering.

terms.gloss: The pre-revolutionary City Governor's chancery, Korobeinikov's former employer.
terms.why_hard: A градоначальник was an Imperial appointed city governor, not a mayor; the contrast with his new Soviet label is the point.

terms.gloss: The Soviet census/personnel euphemism 'worker of office labour', i.e. a clerk.
terms.why_hard: The bureaucratic pomposity is the joke; a plain 'clerk' loses it.

proposed.en: a worker in the field of clerical labour
proposed.zh: 从事办公室劳动的工作者

terms.gloss: The archive keeper, former Tsarist chancery official, who holds the furniture distribution records.
terms.why_hard: Recurring character; the first name is an old church name (Bartholomew) and should be transliterated, not translated.

proposed.zh: 瓦尔福洛梅·科罗贝尼科夫
proposed.ja: ヴァルフォロメイ・コロベイニコフ

conventions: Personal names: one fixed transliteration table for the book; en keeps name-and-patronymic wherever the Russian has it; zh uses 中点 between name parts; ja uses katakana with long-vowel marks on stressed syllables.

Soviet acronyms (Старкомхоз, жилотдел, совторгслужащие): on first occurrence give transliterated acronym plus a short expansion in parentheses, thereafter the acronym alone in en/ja and the short Chinese expansion in zh.

Dialogue dashes become curly double quotes in en and zh (“ ”) and 「 」 in ja; Ostap's mock-official and mock-servile registers (вечер воспоминаний, -с) are rendered in the target's own bureaucratic or polite register, never with footnotes.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The novel's protagonist, a charming young con man introduced on this page; his name is a byword in Russian for a smooth swindler
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Ostap not Ostup, Bender not Bendera); zh/ja must not vary between phonetic variants across chapters

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: The narrators' recurring epithet for Bender: a master of schemes and 'combinations'; also the title of chapter V
terms.why_hard: 'Great combinator' is meaningless in English; needs a phrase that is mock-grand and reusable every time it recurs

terms.gloss: Short for предводитель дворянства, the elected marshal of the nobility of a district or province before 1917; Vorobyaninov's old post
terms.why_hard: Not a military 'leader' or 'chief'; the joke is that the yard-keeper insists on a defunct tsarist rank while Bender calls him a proletarian

terms.gloss: A yard-keeper who swept the courtyard and watched the gate of a house, and his ground-floor lodge; in tsarist times also a police informant
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' or 'doorman' loses the courtyard-and-gate role and the social type; the lodge must not become an 'apartment'

proposed.zh: 扫院人 / 扫院人的小屋

terms.gloss: The old yard-keeper of the Vorobyaninov house in Stargorod, nostalgic for his former master
terms.why_hard: Name must be transliterated consistently; keep Bender's mock-familiar 'дедушка' for him as 'grandad' rather than 'grandfather'

terms.gloss: Bender's orange-coloured laced ankle boots, a recurring visual tag for the character
terms.why_hard: Literally 'orange boots'; the comic word штиблеты (dated, slightly foppish) should get one fixed rendering every time the boots reappear

terms.gloss: Bender's only autobiographical statement: his father was a Turkish subject (i.e. an Odessa merchant who took Ottoman citizenship to escape restrictions); became a Russian proverb for evasive origins
terms.why_hard: Must be a fixed formula since it recurs and is echoed as 'сын турецко-подданного'; not 'a Turk'

proposed.en: My dad was a Turkish subject
proposed.ja: うちの親父はトルコの臣民でした

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town where the chase begins (literally 'Old Town'); home of Vorobyaninov and Tikhon
terms.why_hard: Should be transliterated, not translated, and the same form used in compounds such as Стардеткомиссия

terms.gloss: Stargorod branch of the Children's Commission (Деткомиссия), the Soviet body for aid to homeless children, which funded itself partly by selling pictures and lottery tickets
terms.why_hard: A typical Soviet portmanteau acronym; needs a rendering that keeps the acronym flavour yet tells the reader it is a children's welfare office

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德儿童委员会（斯塔尔儿委会）
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド児童委員会（スタル児童委）

terms.gloss: Bender's planned parody painting: the Soviet leadership answering Austen Chamberlain's 1927 note, a stock propaganda theme after the British break in relations
terms.why_hard: Reader needs to know Chamberlain is the British foreign secretary of 1927, not Neville; a short note is unavoidable

proposed.en: The Bolsheviks Write a Letter to Chamberlain
proposed.ja: 『ボリシェヴィキ、チェンバレンに手紙を書く』

terms.gloss: Repin's famous painting (1891) of Zaporozhian Cossacks composing a mocking reply to the Turkish sultan
terms.why_hard: Use the standard museum title in each language so the reader can recognise the picture; do not translate 'Zaporozhians' as 'Ukrainians'

proposed.en: Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks (the Cossacks Write a Letter to the Sultan)
proposed.zh: 《查波罗什人给土耳其苏丹写信》
proposed.ja: 『トルコのスルタンへ手紙を書くザポロージャ・コサック』

terms.gloss: Ilya Repin, the best-known Russian realist painter
terms.why_hard: Standard forms exist in all three languages; do not respell

terms.gloss: Association of Artists of Revolutionary Russia, the official-realist painters' union of the 1920s whose exhibitions Bender wanders into
terms.why_hard: Bare acronym means nothing to the reader; expand once and reuse the expansion

proposed.en: the AKhRR (Association of Artists of Revolutionary Russia)
proposed.zh: 革命俄罗斯美术家协会
proposed.ja: 革命ロシア美術家協会（アフルル）

terms.gloss: A complimentary pass to a show or exhibition, obtained by acquaintance rather than purchase
terms.why_hard: 'Ticket' loses the point that Bender never pays; 'free pass' or 'comp' keeps it

terms.gloss: A sentence category of the 1926 Soviet criminal code: imprisonment without the stricter 'strict isolation' regime, i.e. a lenient term
terms.why_hard: Tempting to paraphrase as 'two years' probation'; the joke is Bender reading the mildness of the penalty as a business opportunity

proposed.zh: 两年徒刑，不实行严格隔离
proposed.ja: 厳格隔離なしの懲役二年

terms.gloss: A serial bigamist who marries women for their property; Bender's career option no. 1
terms.why_hard: 'Polygamist' keeps the comic literalness; 'bigamist' is the legally accurate but flatter word

terms.gloss: A suit described with the horse-coat term 'dapple-grey', i.e. grey with lighter round spots
terms.why_hard: Literal 'grey with apples' is nonsense; the horse-breeder's word is the joke and should be kept as such

terms.gloss: Marriageable provincial girls likened to Gretchen/Marguerite, Faust's innocent victim in Goethe and Gounod
terms.why_hard: Not a name to transliterate; the allusion is to Faust's Gretchen and the girls' seducibility

proposed.zh: 外省待字闺中的玛格丽特们
proposed.ja: 嫁入り前の田舎のマルガレーテたち

terms.gloss: Bender's professional catchphrase dismissing crude, inelegant swindles
terms.why_hard: Recurs verbatim; the trade-grading tone ('low grade') should be fixed once

terms.gloss: Mikhail Kalinin, titular head of the Soviet state, and Georgy Chicherin, commissar for foreign affairs; 'т.' abbreviates товарищ
terms.why_hard: The abbreviation must be rendered as 'Comrade', and the bald names need a note so the reader gets the joke of undressing the foreign minister

proposed.zh: 加里宁同志 / 契切林同志
proposed.ja: カリーニン同志 / チチェーリン同志

terms.gloss: Tall Caucasian sheepskin hat and white felt cloak, the costume of Repin's Cossack chieftain
terms.why_hard: Generic 'fur hat and cloak' loses the Cossack picture the reader must see

proposed.en: a tall Cossack fur hat and a white felt cloak
proposed.zh: 高筒羊皮帽和白色毡斗篷
proposed.ja: コサック風の毛皮帽と白いフェルトの外套

terms.gloss: Chief of police of a tsarist provincial town; Tikhon boasts that this official saluted his master
terms.why_hard: Not 'policeman'; it is the top police rank in town, which is the point of the boast

terms.gloss: Colloquial for a three-ruble note, the customary holiday tip
terms.why_hard: Keep the sum concrete; 'a tip' loses the arithmetic of Tikhon's fifteen rubles a year

terms.gloss: Name day, the feast of one's patron saint, celebrated like a birthday in pre-revolutionary Russia
terms.why_hard: Not 'birthday' and not literally 'angel's day'; Tikhon's respectful plural 'ихнего' also marks his servant's speech

proposed.ja: 名の日（守護聖人の祝日）

terms.gloss: Tikhon's verbal tic, a filler meaning 'let's say, so to speak', repeated in every speech of his
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed filler phrase so his voice is recognisable, not smoothed away

proposed.ja: たとえばだな、言ってみりゃ

chapter_titles.45: Глава XII. Знойная женщина — мечта поэта

meta.summary: object with keys [conventions, chapter_titles, writers]

terms.gloss: Mock-epithet for the Stargorod correspondent whose pen-name is Маховик (Flywheel); 'Prince' and 'of Denmark' pun on Hamlet, Prince of Denmark.
terms.why_hard: Both halves must keep the Hamlet echo and the pen-name; rendering 'Datsky' as a surname or dropping 'Prince' kills the joke and breaks the link to the Маховик pen-name used earlier in the chapter.

proposed.ja: フライホイール王子／デンマークのフライホイール

terms.gloss: Pen-name of the local Stargorod newspaper correspondent (literally 'flywheel').
terms.why_hard: It is a pseudonym, not a surname, so it should be translated as a word, consistently, and match the 'Prince Flywheel' epithet.

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town ('Old Town') where the first part of the novel is set.
terms.why_hard: A fictional toponym; transliterate consistently rather than translate, and keep it distinct from real places.

terms.gloss: Chairman of the Stargorod communal-services board, the well-meaning speaker who drifts into the 'international situation'.
terms.why_hard: Consistent transliteration; his speech is ungrammatical and folksy and must sound so in every language.

terms.gloss: Chief engineer who built the Stargorod tram line; the honest 'Soviet specialist'.
terms.why_hard: Consistent transliteration across chapters; name is on the edge of comic (треух = ear-flap hat) but should not be translated.

terms.gloss: The novel's con-man protagonist, 'the great schemer'.
terms.why_hard: Standard transliteration is established (Ostap Bender); zh/ja should follow existing published translations, not ad-hoc phonetics.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary; villain of 1927 Soviet propaganda ('Our answer to Chamberlain') after Britain broke off relations.
terms.why_hard: Not Neville Chamberlain; the reader needs to know he was the stock bogeyman of every 1927 Soviet speech, hence the joke of giving him half an hour.

terms.gloss: William Borah, US senator, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, frequently mentioned in Soviet press of the 1920s.
terms.why_hard: Obscure today; transliteration must match the real name (Borah) so a curious reader can look him up.

terms.gloss: 'Romanian boyars', Soviet propaganda cliché for the Romanian ruling class that had annexed Bessarabia.
terms.why_hard: Must keep the archaic 'boyars' rather than 'landowners' to preserve the newspaper-slogan flavour.

proposed.zh: 罗马尼亚的贵族老爷们
proposed.ja: ルーマニアの大貴族ども

terms.gloss: 'The international situation', the stock topic every Soviet speaker of the 1920s felt obliged to cover.
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed phrase throughout so the running joke (Gavrilin's 'second, international nature') lands; do not vary it.

terms.gloss: Abbreviation of the All-Russian Union of Dairy Cooperatives, the central butter-marketing organisation of the NEP years.
terms.why_hard: A real acronym-organisation; rendering as a proper noun leaves the reader baffled, so expand it lightly ('Butter Centre') and keep it the same everywhere.

terms.term: Трамвай построить — это не ешака купить
terms.gloss: Gavrilin's homely opening: 'building a tram line is not like buying a donkey' (ешак = dialect for ишак, a donkey).
terms.why_hard: The word is sub-standard and rustic; a neutral 'donkey' loses the peasant flavour that makes Ostap laugh.

proposed.en: Building a tramway ain't like buying a donkey.
proposed.ja: 電車を作るってのは、ロバを買うのとは訳が違う。

terms.term: не за страх, а за совесть
terms.gloss: Proverbial: to work 'not out of fear but out of conscience', i.e. wholeheartedly.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering sounds odd; needs a fixed idiomatic equivalent, since it recurs in Soviet speech parodies.

proposed.en: not for fear but for conscience's sake
proposed.zh: 不是出于害怕，而是出于良心
proposed.ja: 恐れからではなく、良心から

terms.gloss: Subbotniks: 'voluntary' unpaid collective work days (originally Saturdays) in the early Soviet period.
terms.why_hard: Not simply 'Saturdays' or 'overtime'; keep the loanword with a brief gloss on first occurrence.

proposed.ja: 土曜労働奉仕（スボートニク）

terms.gloss: Stock Soviet newspaper formula for reporting speeches: 'stormy applause turning into an ovation'.
terms.why_hard: Must read as recognisable press boilerplate, not fresh prose; the same wording should be used wherever the cliché recurs.

proposed.en: Stormy applause, turning into an ovation
proposed.zh: 热烈的掌声，转为经久不息的欢呼
proposed.ja: 万雷の拍手、やがて大喝采へ

terms.gloss: Another journalistic cliché ('in vivid terms the speaker outlined…') the two correspondents write in unison.
terms.why_hard: The parody depends on it sounding like tired reportage in the target language, not like the narrator.

proposed.en: In vivid terms the speaker outlined the international situation of our Union
proposed.zh: 演讲者以生动的语言描绘了我们联盟的国际形势
proposed.ja: 演説者は我が連邦の国際情勢を生き生きと描き出した

terms.gloss: A short brass fanfare/flourish played by a band to salute a speaker or toast.
terms.why_hard: Not 'ink' (тушь) and not a whole piece of music; 'flourish' or 'fanfare' is needed, consistently.

terms.gloss: Formulaic chairing phrase: 'the floor is given to…'.
terms.why_hard: Use the same formal meeting formula each time it appears; it marks Soviet meeting ritual.

proposed.ja: 次に……に発言を願います

terms.gloss: The 'honest Soviet specialist': NEP-era term for a pre-revolutionary-trained expert (spets) working loyally for the regime.
terms.why_hard: 'Specialist' in English is bland; the phrase is a political category, so keep 'specialist' and gloss once.

proposed.ja: 誠実なソヴィエトの専門家

terms.gloss: 'Comrades', the standard Soviet form of address, here padding nearly every clause of Gavrilin's speech.
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered identically everywhere and kept every time it repeats, since the repetition is the joke.

terms.gloss: A refrigerated slaughterhouse/meat-packing plant, a typical 1920s compound-word project name.
terms.why_hard: Keep the bureaucratic compound flavour rather than plain 'slaughterhouse'.

terms.gloss: Gavrilin declines the indeclinable loanword 'депо' (tram depot), a marker of his half-education.
terms.why_hard: The error should be mirrored by a small grammatical slip in the target, not silently corrected.

terms.gloss: The unnamed young correspondent from Moscow, contrasted with the local Flywheel.
terms.why_hard: Use one fixed label ('the Muscovite') so the two-journalist contrast stays legible.

conventions: Newspaper clichés quoted in «…» are rendered as flat press boilerplate in each language and set in quotation marks, distinct from the narrator's voice.
Dialogue dashes become English double quotes, Chinese “…”, Japanese 「…」; Gavrilin's ungrammatical speech keeps small deliberate errors in every language.
Names are transliterated (not translated) except pen-names and epithets like Маховик/Принц-Маховик, which are translated as words; Japanese uses no honorifics for Russian names.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's name-and-patronymic, the narrator's default way of naming him
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed transliteration; a careless translator drops the patronymic or alternates it with the surname at random, and the mock-respectful full form is part of the joke

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Surname of the former marshal of the nobility, the novel's co-protagonist
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must match everywhere (ь, я); the narrator switches between surname, name-patronymic and 'предводитель' for the same man on one page

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man, 'the great combinator'
terms.why_hard: One fixed form; do not anglicise to 'Ostap' variants or use surname where the text uses first name

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the parish priest who learned of the jewels in confession and hunts them independently
terms.why_hard: Federal 'Fyodor'/'Fedor' spelling and the 'Father' title must be fixed; zh/ja need a priest-title that reads Orthodox, not Catholic 'padre'

terms.gloss: 'Holy father' - the narrator's mock-reverent epithet for Father Fyodor, used while he is kicking people in the groin
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered with the same deadpan solemnity every time; zh '圣父' means God the Father and is wrong

terms.gloss: Familiar Russian address/reference for an Orthodox priest ('Father'), used both in narration and in Vorobyaninov's 'Стыдно, батюшка!'
terms.why_hard: Different register from 'святой отец' and 'отец Федор'; a translator who flattens all three to 'the priest' loses the narrator's shifting irony

terms.gloss: Short for предводитель дворянства, the elected pre-revolutionary marshal of the nobility; the narrator keeps calling Vorobyaninov by his abolished rank
terms.why_hard: Not 'leader' or 'chief'; the joke is a Soviet citizen in 1927 still tagged with a tsarist office. Fix a short form usable dozens of times

terms.term: технический директор и главный руководитель концессии
terms.gloss: Bender's self-awarded corporate title for his role in the treasure hunt, which he styles a 'concession'
terms.why_hard: Part of a fixed set of mock-business titles (концессия, концессионер, компаньон) that must stay parallel across the whole book; do not paraphrase as 'the con man'

proposed.en: technical director and chief executive of the concession
proposed.zh: 特许公司技术总监兼总经理
proposed.ja: コンセッションの技術部長兼総責任者

terms.gloss: NEP-era term for a private (often foreign) enterprise licensed by the state; Bender's running name for the chair hunt and for himself
terms.why_hard: The NEP business flavour is the joke; 'partnership' or 'scheme' loses it, and the word recurs through the whole novel

proposed.zh: 特许公司 / 总特许经营人
proposed.ja: コンセッション / コンセッション総代表

terms.gloss: 'Business partner' - how the narrator labels Bender relative to Vorobyaninov, continuing the corporate parody
terms.why_hard: Should be a business word, not 'companion' or 'friend'

terms.gloss: Property confiscated by the Soviet state after 1917; here the priest's absurd legal claim to the chair
terms.why_hard: Keep the exact bureaucratic phrase so the shouted repetition works; do not soften to 'public property'

terms.term: Советская власть / власть трудящихся / власть рабочих и крестьян
terms.gloss: Official formulas for the Soviet regime ('Soviet power', 'power of the toilers', 'workers' and peasants' power') that the priest recites like a catechism
terms.why_hard: Three slogans in escalating order; translate each with its standard propaganda equivalent, consistently book-wide, rather than merging them into 'the government'

proposed.en: Soviet power / the power of the working people / the workers' and peasants' power
proposed.zh: 苏维埃政权 / 劳动人民政权 / 工农政权
proposed.ja: ソヴィエト政権 / 勤労者の権力 / 労農政権

terms.gloss: 'A Party member' (of the Communist Party); Vorobyaninov's horrified accusation against a priest
terms.why_hard: Must read as the one Party; 'political' or 'partisan' misses the joke

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary deferential particle -с ('sir') attached to words; marks the old-regime manners both men still carry
terms.why_hard: Untranslatable literally; needs one fixed device (an archaic 'sir', an obsequious verb ending) used whenever -с appears in the book

proposed.ja: さようで、さようでございます

terms.gloss: Жилищный отдел - the municipal housing department that redistributed furniture and rooms; a Soviet acronym-word
terms.why_hard: Acronym must be unpacked into a recognizable office, and the same rendering used for every жил-/-отдел acronym in the book

terms.gloss: Almshouse - the Stargorod old women's home ('2nd House of Social Security') from which a chair was bought
terms.why_hard: Refers back to a specific institution seen earlier; rendering must match the earlier chapters

terms.gloss: Street named for the 1912 Lena goldfields massacre - a typical Soviet renaming of a provincial street
terms.why_hard: The comedy is a sleepy town with a revolutionary-martyrdom street name; must be identifiable as such, not transliterated as 'Lenskikh Sobyty Street'

terms.gloss: Yerofeyev Lane, an old-fashioned pre-revolutionary street name crossing the renamed one
terms.why_hard: Contrast with the Soviet name should survive; keep 'lane' for переулок throughout the book

terms.gloss: The shimmy, a 1920s Western dance craze, and the nonsense 'batacudas' of a popular Soviet foxtrot lyric Bender hums
terms.why_hard: The verse needs a fixed rendering with its hyphenated stutter kept; the dance name should be the target language's own 1920s term

proposed.zh: 希米舞 / 巴-塔-库-达人
proposed.ja: シミー / バ・タ・ク・ダ族

terms.gloss: 'Only horns and hooves were left' - from the nursery song about grandma's grey goat eaten by wolves; here punning on ножки = chair legs
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering loses the song; a plain 'nothing was left' loses the pun on legs. Choose one and use it wherever the idiom recurs

proposed.en: nothing was left of it but horns and legs
proposed.zh: 只剩下几只角和几条腿
proposed.ja: 残ったのは角と脚だけだった

terms.gloss: 'Your arms are too short' - you lack the power/reach to do that
terms.why_hard: Literal 'short hands' is meaningless; needs a defiant colloquial retort

proposed.ja: そんな力はないくせに

terms.gloss: Wrestling term: the bout continued 'on the mat' (ground wrestling); партер also means theatre stalls
terms.why_hard: The mock sports-report register is the joke; do not render as 'in the stalls' or 'on the ground' flatly

proposed.en: the bout continued on the mat

terms.gloss: 'Treasure-hunters' and the 'walnut treasure-vault' (the chair) - narrator's mock-epic labels for the two men and the chair
terms.why_hard: Recurring epic epithet for the pair; rendering must stay stable and keep the mock-solemn tone

proposed.zh: 寻宝者 / 核桃木宝库
proposed.ja: 宝探しの二人 / クルミ材の宝物庫

terms.gloss: The seal of confession, which Father Fyodor broke to learn of the jewels
terms.why_hard: Use the established ecclesiastical term, not 'confession secret'

terms.gloss: Swindler, shady operator - a NEP-era insult that also fits Bender
terms.why_hard: Keep one word for it book-wide since it is thrown at several characters

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash speech becomes double quotation marks in en, “ ” in zh, 「 」 in ja; the narrator's interjections inside a speech stay inline, not as separate lines.

Vorobyaninov and Father Fyodor keep formal вы even while brawling and spitting; render with full 'Father'/'Ippolit Matveyevich' address in en, 您 in zh, and です/ます plus 神父 in ja, so the comic politeness survives.

Bender's corporate parody vocabulary (концессия, концессионер, технический директор, компаньон) is a fixed set rendered with business terms and never explained or varied; Russian names are transliterated consistently without added Japanese honorifics.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, parish priest of Stargorod who is the third, hapless competitor for the chairs; recurs through the whole novel
terms.why_hard: Name must be one fixed transliteration book-wide (Fyodor, not Fedor/Theodore); 'отец' is a clerical title, not 'father' as parent

terms.gloss: the Vostrikovs, Father Fyodor's family name (used of the household's trunk)
terms.why_hard: Surname appears rarely; must match the transliteration used wherever Vostrikov recurs

terms.gloss: customary title of address for an Orthodox priest's wife (paired with 'батюшка'); also used by the narrator as her designation
terms.why_hard: Not 'mother' or 'little mother'; the reader needs to know she is the priest's wife, and the same word is both vocative and narrative label

proposed.en: Mother (in address) / the priest's wife (in narration)
proposed.zh: 娘子（称呼）/ 神父太太（叙述）
proposed.ja: 母さん（呼びかけ）/ 神父の妻（地の文）

terms.gloss: the priest's wife, a plainer and slightly comic everyday word the narrator alternates with 'матушка'
terms.why_hard: Translators tend to merge it with матушка or invent a title; the narrator's shift to the blunter word is a deadpan touch worth keeping

terms.gloss: affectionate diminutive of Fyodor used by his wife
terms.why_hard: A distinct form from 'Федор'; must not be rendered as a different name, and the tenderness should survive

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor's wife, name plus patronymic, used when he gives her orders
terms.why_hard: Full name-and-patronymic marks formality; a fixed transliteration is needed and the patronymic must not be treated as a surname

proposed.zh: 卡捷琳娜·亚历山德罗夫娜
proposed.ja: カテリーナ・アレクサンドロヴナ

terms.gloss: the Renovationists ('Living Church'), a Soviet-tolerated schismatic reform movement in the Orthodox Church of the 1920s, associated with modern dress, short hair, divorce and worldly habits
terms.why_hard: A term the 1928 reader knew; 'reformers' or 'modernists' loses the specific schism, and the joke about cinemas and alimony depends on it

terms.gloss: an old-fashioned 1910s word for a cinema, still current in the provinces
terms.why_hard: Not 'illusion'; the dated word is part of the wife's provincial voice, so a plain 'cinema' flattens it

terms.gloss: Renovationist clergy could divorce and remarry, hence pay alimony; the wife's barb
terms.why_hard: The punchline lands only if the reader gets that a priest paying alimony is scandalous; may need a one-line note

terms.gloss: the priest's cassock, under which he wears striped civilian trousers
terms.why_hard: Must be consistently 'cassock', not 'robe' or 'gown', and the striped trousers underneath are the joke

terms.gloss: civilian (lay) clothes as opposed to clerical dress
terms.why_hard: 'Civilian' works for a priest only if the reader already knows clerical dress is a uniform; 'lay clothes' may be clearer

terms.gloss: a peaked cap with a long flat 'duck-bill' visor, typical lower-middle-class headgear
terms.why_hard: Literal 'duck cap' is nonsense; the object is a flat cap, and the wife calls it 'дурацкий' (idiotic) so the rendering should sound slightly ridiculous

terms.gloss: overcoat with a curly lambskin (astrakhan-style) collar, a respectable tradesman's coat
terms.why_hard: 'Sheepskin collar' misreads it as a peasant coat; the collar is the baker's mark of prosperity

terms.gloss: Red Army soldiers, whose tin-bound trunks decorated with pictures are described
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed rendering book-wide; 'Red Army men' (not 'soldiers of the Red Army') keeps the period flavor

terms.gloss: Semyon Budyonny, Civil War cavalry commander and Soviet icon, famous for his huge moustache; his portrait was standard decoration
terms.why_hard: A name the reader will not know; needs a consistent transliteration and a very brief gloss the first time, and the moustache echoes Father Fyodor's

terms.gloss: box of 'Beach' brand papirosy (cardboard-tube cigarettes) with three bathing beauties on the lid
terms.why_hard: Папиросы recur throughout the book and are not Western cigarettes; the brand name should be translated, not transliterated

terms.gloss: Batum (Batumi), Black Sea resort in Soviet Georgia, the pebbly beach on the cigarette box
terms.why_hard: Period spelling Batum vs modern Batumi must be chosen once; the reader needs to sense 'seaside resort'

terms.gloss: an illustrated patriotic weekly of the First World War, source of the trunk's cut-out photographs
terms.why_hard: Periodical titles need one fixed translated form and one bracket convention across languages

terms.gloss: caption of a photo of the Russian capture of the Austrian fortress Przemyśl (March 1915)
terms.why_hard: Russian 'Перемышль' vs Polish Przemyśl: pick a spelling the reader can look up

terms.gloss: 'lower ranks', official Imperial Army term for enlisted men, here in a mock-official photo caption
terms.why_hard: 'Lower ranks' sounds like a mistranslation; the bureaucratic flavor of the caption is the point

terms.gloss: The Russian Pilgrim, a pre-revolutionary religious illustrated weekly; a 1903 set lies in the trunk

terms.why_hard: 'Schism' without qualifier reads as the East-West schism to a Western reader; a short note or 'Old Believer' gloss may be needed

terms.gloss: gold ten-rouble coins of the imperial period, hoarded as hard money in the NEP years

terms.gloss: three- and five-rouble Soviet banknotes
terms.why_hard: Denominations recur throughout; choose one pattern for '-рублевка' notes

proposed.zh: 三卢布和五卢布的票子
proposed.ja: 三ルーブル札と五ルーブル札

terms.gloss: the narrator's mock-solemn label for the priest's series of failed get-rich schemes, a running motif
terms.why_hard: The dry phrase recurs; render it the same way each time so the reader hears the refrain

proposed.zh: 费奥多尔神父的商业冒险
proposed.ja: フョードル神父の商業的冒険

terms.gloss: an old-fashioned woman's bonnet tied under the chin, long out of fashion by 1928
terms.why_hard: 'Hat' or 'hood' loses the datedness that makes it the right hiding place

conventions: Personal names: one fixed transliteration table per language (en BGN-style without diacritics, zh standard 新华社 forms, ja katakana with ・ between name and patronymic); diminutives (Феденька) kept as transliterated forms, not replaced by the base name.

Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become quoted speech (en double quotes, zh “”, ja 「」); ты/вы between the priest and his wife is intimate ты and needs no marking, but ja uses plain forms between spouses and です/ます only where вы is used.
Titles of books and periodicals: en italics, zh 《》, ja 『』; photo captions and brand names in en single quotes, zh “”, ja 《》, with the title translated rather than transliterated.

terms.gloss: Ostap's fake monarchist conspiracy; орало is archaic 'ploughshare' (Isaiah 2:4 'swords into ploughshares'), so the name is a mock-heraldic oxymoron
terms.why_hard: Орало is not 'oral' or 'plough' in a modern sense; the biblical echo and mock-solemnity must survive, and the name recurs as the chapter title and in Kislyarsky's fears

proposed.en: the Union of the Sword and the Ploughshare

terms.gloss: Ostap's recurring mock-grandiose epithet for Vorobyaninov
terms.why_hard: Became a Russian proverb; must be rendered identically every time, keeping the pomposity, not paraphrased as 'great thinker'

terms.gloss: Second half of Ostap's fixed epithet for Vorobyaninov, absurd for a former marshal of the nobility
terms.why_hard: Fixed formula that recurs book-wide; the irony is in its literalness, so translate literally and consistently

terms.gloss: Third element of the epithet: 'a personage close to the Emperor', pre-revolutionary court language
terms.why_hard: Особа is formal court/official register, not just 'person'; keep the stiff officialese

proposed.en: a personage close to the Emperor

terms.gloss: Ostap's one-word recruiting refrain to each conspirator: 'bear up / stand firm'
terms.why_hard: The comedy is mechanical repetition; every occurrence must use the same rendering, and it should sound like consolation at a funeral, not a pep talk

proposed.ja: 気をしっかりお持ちください。

terms.gloss: Ostap's refrain (variant: Запад нам поможет), a parody of émigré/monarchist hopes; now a Russian proverb
terms.why_hard: Заграница is 'abroad' as a collective actor; both variants must be recognisably the same slogan

proposed.en: Abroad will help us. / The West will help us.
proposed.zh: 外国会帮助我们。/ 西方会帮助我们。
proposed.ja: 外国が助けてくれます。／西側が助けてくれます。

terms.term: Полная тайна вкладов, то есть организации
terms.gloss: Ostap's slip: 'полная тайна вкладов' was the Soviet savings-bank slogan ('secrecy of deposits'), which he corrects to 'of the organisation'
terms.why_hard: The joke depends on the reader recognising the bank slogan; the recurring 'Полная тайна организации' must match this line

proposed.en: Total secrecy of deposits—of the organisation, that is.
proposed.zh: 存款绝对保密——我是说，组织绝对保密。
proposed.ja: 預金の秘密は厳守…いや、組織の秘密は厳守です。

terms.gloss: 'The only hold-up is public opinion', i.e. we lack only local support
terms.why_hard: Остановка за + instr. = 'the only thing lacking is'; not 'a stop for public opinion'

proposed.en: All that's lacking is public opinion.

terms.gloss: 'Our reach is long' — threat that the organisation can punish deserters anywhere
terms.why_hard: Chinese 手长 connotes greed/pilfering, so it must be recast as reach; it is quoted back in the narration ('длинные руки' произвели невыгодное впечатление) so the quote must match

terms.gloss: Elected member of a pre-revolutionary municipal council (city duma)
terms.why_hard: Гласный is not 'vowel' or 'public'; a target reader needs 'city councillor' without a footnote, plus the old regime flavour

proposed.en: former councillor of the old City Duma
proposed.ja: 元市会（市ドゥーマ）議員

terms.gloss: Ostap's recruiting question implying tsarist officer past; nobles were expected to have served
terms.why_hard: Recurs verbatim to each recruit; keep identical and formal so the parody of White-officer vetting reads

proposed.en: What regiment did you serve in?
proposed.ja: どの連隊におられましたか。

terms.gloss: Member of the hereditary nobility, a legal estate abolished in 1917 ('Да. Был.')
terms.why_hard: 'Nobleman' must carry the sense of a legal category one could cease to be, so 'Yes. I was.' lands

terms.gloss: The Imperial Guards regiments, elite units where nobles served
terms.why_hard: Not 'guard' in a security sense; use the established 'Guards'

terms.gloss: A NEP-era private firm, mock-Soviet contraction of быстрая упаковка 'quick packing'
terms.why_hard: The name parodies Soviet acronyms; a bare transliteration loses the joke, a full translation loses the Soviet sound

proposed.ja: 「ブィストロウパク」（速梱包社）

terms.gloss: Soviet-press label for a NEP private businessman (NEPman), here used by Ostap with mock respect
terms.why_hard: Sounds like officialese in Russian; keep the newspaper register rather than 'businessman'

terms.gloss: Sentence category of the 1926 RSFSR Criminal Code: imprisonment with strict isolation
terms.why_hard: Legal term of art, not 'solitary confinement'; Kislyarsky's mental sentencing escalates to 'десять лет', so both must read as criminal-code language

terms.gloss: Narrator's jab: Nikesha and Vladya are 'fully ripened' bunglers, i.e. grown-up nitwits
terms.why_hard: Недотепа is colloquial 'hapless clod'; the mock-agricultural 'ripened' must be kept

proposed.ja: すっかり熟した間抜け

terms.gloss: 'Ostap was carried away' — his patter is running on its own momentum
terms.why_hard: Impersonal несло; not 'Ostap was carrying'; keep the sense of an uncontrolled current

proposed.ja: オスタップは止まらなくなった。

terms.term: под каким соусом все это будет подано
terms.gloss: 'Under what sauce it will be served' — how the scheme is dressed up
terms.why_hard: Food metaphor common in Russian; render as presentation, keep the sauce if idiomatic

proposed.en: what sauce it's all served up in
proposed.zh: 这一切端上来时浇的是什么酱
proposed.ja: どんなソースで出されるか

terms.gloss: Chicken gizzards (southern/Odessa cooking), part of Kislyarsky's remembered good dinner
terms.why_hard: Literal 'chicken belly-buttons' is wrong; it is a homely delicacy

terms.gloss: Soviet address 'citizen' vs pre-revolutionary 'mister'; Kislyarsky's 'господин' betrays old-regime loyalty
terms.why_hard: Both forms must be distinguished consistently book-wide, since the contrast is a running joke

proposed.zh: 公民基斯利亚尔斯基 / 沃罗比亚尼诺夫先生
proposed.ja: 市民キスリャルスキー／ヴォロビヤニノフ殿

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, co-protagonist; narrator calls him by name-and-patronymic
terms.why_hard: Name-and-patronymic must be kept, not replaced by surname; transliteration fixed book-wide

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the con man
terms.why_hard: Fixed transliteration; do not anglicise to 'Ostap Bender' every time when the text has just 'Остап'

terms.gloss: The hyperactive Stargorod locksmith-intellectual who gathers the conspirators
terms.why_hard: Narrator alternates 'Полесов' and 'Виктор Михайлович'; both forms must map to one person consistently

proposed.zh: 维克多·米哈伊洛维奇·波列索夫
proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

terms.gloss: Two dim young men (diminutives of Nikifor and Vladimir), Polesov's recruits
terms.why_hard: Diminutives signal childishness at age thirty; keep the diminutive forms, do not expand to full names

proposed.ja: ニケーシャとヴラージャ

terms.gloss: Fat old former city councillor, one of the conspirators
terms.why_hard: Fixed transliteration

terms.gloss: Timid NEP businessman, perpetually expecting arrest
terms.why_hard: Fixed transliteration

terms.gloss: Fortune-teller in whose flat the conspiracy meets
terms.why_hard: Fixed transliteration; name-and-patronymic only, never a surname

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

conventions: Ostap's recruiting formulas (Крепитесь; В каком полку служили?; Заграница/Запад нам поможет; Полная тайна организации) are rendered with one fixed wording per language everywhere in the book, since the comedy is repetition

Dialogue dashes become English double quotes, Chinese “ ”, Japanese 「 」; the narrator's asides and characters' inner speech in «» stay as quotation marks (en single, zh “ ”, ja 「 」) rather than italics

Japanese: narrator in plain form (だ・である), Ostap addresses recruits in polite です・ます with mock-solemn ください; Russian names kept in katakana with long vowels marked and name-and-patronymic preserved where the Russian uses it

terms.gloss: the unnamed provincial district town where the novel opens; 'uezd' is the pre-revolutionary county-level unit, still in use in 1927
terms.why_hard: the Gogolian 'town of N' convention must be kept as a letter, not expanded to a name; 'uezd' should read as a small county seat, not 'county' in the US sense

terms.gloss: protagonist, 52, former marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk; the narrator almost always uses name+patronymic
terms.why_hard: transliteration and patronymic form must be fixed once (Matveyevich vs Matveevich); zh/ja need a stable multi-character transcription used identically hundreds of times

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャーニノフ

terms.gloss: Klavdiya Ivanovna Petukhova, Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law, who sewed the jewels into the chair
terms.why_hard: she is referred to by name+patronymic only; translators must not add 'Mrs' or a surname the text withholds here

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: the town's coffin-maker, a recurring comic figure with a taxonomy of ways to die
terms.why_hard: surname appears in the chapter title; spelling must match across all chapters and the 'нимфы' rivals

terms.gloss: archaic trade title 'master of coffin affairs', i.e. undertaker/coffin-maker, styled like a pre-revolutionary shop sign
terms.why_hard: flattening to 'undertaker' loses the mock-solemn sign-board register that the narrator quotes

terms.gloss: the rival funeral parlour whose staff Bezenchuk calls 'the nymphs'; gives the chapter its title
terms.why_hard: the shop name must be kept as a proper name in quotes, and the plural 'нимфы' for its staff must be derivable from it in each language

terms.term: бюро похоронных процессий / похоронных депо / погребальная контора
terms.gloss: three pompous NEP-era euphemisms for a funeral business, varied deliberately for comic effect
terms.why_hard: a translator who normalises all to 'funeral home' kills the joke of bureaucratic over-naming; each variant needs its own stable rendering

proposed.en: funeral-procession bureau / funeral depots / burial office
proposed.zh: 殡葬仪式事务所 / 殡仪站 / 埋葬事务处
proposed.ja: 葬列取扱所 / 葬儀ステーション / 埋葬事務所

terms.gloss: name of a bankrupt funeral office; the phrase is a hospitable 'you are most welcome / do come in', grotesque on a coffin shop
terms.why_hard: must be translated as a phrase (the joke) not transliterated, and kept as a sign in capitals

terms.gloss: vegetal, a perfumed barber's hair lotion of the period
terms.why_hard: obscure even to modern Russians; should be rendered as a recognisable barbershop lotion, not a literal 'vegetable'

terms.gloss: mestkom = local trade-union committee; of the municipal-services workers' union
terms.why_hard: the acronym must expand to something a non-Soviet reader parses at once, and 'communal' must not suggest communists

proposed.zh: 市政公用事业工会基层委员会
proposed.ja: 公共事業労働組合の地方委員会

terms.gloss: trade-union membership dues collected by the local committee secretary
terms.why_hard: must stay recognisably union dues, not club fees or taxes

terms.gloss: street 'named after Comrade Gubernsky', a joke: the surname is the adjective 'provincial/gubernia'
terms.why_hard: the pun on 'gubernia' cannot be transliterated silently; keep the Soviet 'named after Comrade X' formula and preserve the name so the joke can be noted once

proposed.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

terms.gloss: barbershop sign using the archaic 'tsirulnik' (barber-surgeon) and a fake-French owner name
terms.why_hard: the pretension is in the archaic title and the French 'Pierre' beside a plain 'Konstantin'; a flat 'barber' loses it

proposed.zh: “皮埃尔与康斯坦丁理容大师”
proposed.ja: 「理髪師匠 ピエールとコンスタンチン」

terms.gloss: mangled provincial gallicisms on a shop sign: manicure and ondulation (hair waving) at home
terms.why_hard: the comedy is the garbled foreign words; render as slightly pretentious salon-speak, not as correct modern 'manicure'

proposed.en: nail-grooming and ondulation at your home
proposed.ja: 爪のお手入れ、ご自宅で電髪

terms.gloss: to drink hard, be on a drinking bout (literally 'drink the bitter one', i.e. vodka)
terms.why_hard: a literal 'drank bitter' is meaningless; needs an idiomatic equivalent for heavy habitual drinking

terms.gloss: the (state) pawnshop of the NEP era
terms.why_hard: ordinary 'pawnshop' is fine but must be consistent, as pawning recurs as a plot device

terms.gloss: ZAGS, the Soviet civil registry office for births, deaths and marriages, where Vorobyaninov works
terms.why_hard: an acronym the target reader does not know; expand it rather than transliterate, and keep one expansion book-wide

terms.gloss: the 'desk' (sub-department) for deaths and marriages inside the registry office; 'стол' also puns with his literal table
terms.why_hard: 'desk' must be usable both as a department and as the physical table the next paragraph describes as a tombstone

terms.gloss: pince-nez spectacles clipped to the nose, Vorobyaninov's signature prop throughout the book
terms.why_hard: must be kept distinct from 'очки' (spectacles), since the passage contrasts them

terms.gloss: Pavel Milyukov, liberal Kadet leader and 1917 foreign minister, famous for his rimless spectacles; the wife's comparison is a slur
terms.why_hard: unknown to the target reader; needs a brief in-text gloss or note on why looking like him is undesirable in 1927

proposed.zh: 米留科夫（流亡的自由派政客）
proposed.ja: ミリュコーフ（亡命した自由主義派の政治家）

terms.gloss: the building yard-keeper, a low-status figure who sweeps, guards and reports; recurs across the novel
terms.why_hard: 'janitor' or 'doorman' each miss part of the role; choose one rendering and keep it

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's mood barometer: French greeting when cheerful, German when his liver aches
terms.why_hard: must remain foreign words in Cyrillic-style rendering, not translated to 'Good morning', or the contrast disappears

proposed.zh: “邦茹尔”（法语早安）/ “古特摩根”（德语早安）
proposed.ja: 「ボンジュール」／「グーテン・モルゲン」

terms.gloss: his liver is 'playing up', a colloquial hypochondriac's complaint
terms.why_hard: keep the light colloquial tone rather than a medical statement

conventions: Russian dialogue dashes become English double quotation marks, Chinese “ ” and Japanese 「 」; the narrator's parenthetical asides stay in parentheses in all three languages.

Name + patronymic is kept in full where the Russian has it (Ippolit Matveyevich), transliterated by a single fixed table; zh uses · between name parts, ja uses ・ and no honorifics (no さん) since the narrator uses none.

Soviet acronyms (загс, местком) are expanded to a plain descriptive phrase on first and every occurrence rather than transliterated; a translator's note is used only for allusions to real people (Milyukov) that no rendering can carry.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The protagonist, former marshal of the nobility, addressed by name and patronymic throughout the book
terms.why_hard: Transliteration drifts (Ippolit/Hippolyte, Matveevich/Matveyevich); the name-and-patronymic form must be kept as one fixed unit in all three languages

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's surname; Bezenchuk calls him 'господин Воробьянинов'
terms.why_hard: Surname contains воробей (sparrow) but must not be translated; spelling must match the patronymic form everywhere

terms.gloss: The coffin-maker of Stargorod, a recurring comic character who reappears later in the book
terms.why_hard: Recurring name; his dialect speech (ежели, неужто, значит) must get a fixed low-colloquial register that later pages reuse

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's mother-in-law, Madame Petukhova, whose death opens the plot
terms.why_hard: Referred to by name-patronymic, as 'мадам Петухова', as 'теща' and as 'старушка'; all four must map to one person consistently

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: Chapter-title form of the mother-in-law's name; 'мадам' is a pre-revolutionary bourgeois honorific used mock-solemnly
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as plain 'Mrs' loses the deliberate old-regime flavour the narrator is mocking

terms.gloss: Mock-formal trade title, 'master of coffin affairs', modelled on pre-revolutionary guild titles like 'часовых дел мастер'
terms.why_hard: Flattening to 'undertaker' kills the pompous guild-title joke that the whole death-vocabulary scene builds on

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk addresses the ex-noble with the pre-revolutionary 'gospodin', anachronistic and obsequious in 1927
terms.why_hard: Must be kept distinct from 'товарищ' and 'гражданин' so the reader senses the old-regime deference

proposed.ja: ヴォロビヤニノフの旦那

terms.gloss: Orthodox formula said on hearing of a death, 'may she inherit the Kingdom of Heaven'
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering sounds like theology; it is a reflexive pious interjection like 'God rest her'

proposed.ja: 天国に召されますように

terms.gloss: Church-Slavonic verb for dying, first rung of Bezenchuk's ladder: for small, plump old women
terms.why_hard: The whole passage is a graded taxonomy of death-verbs; each rung needs its own fixed phrase that recurs later when Bezenchuk reappears

terms.gloss: 'Gives up her soul to God', for larger, thinner old women in Bezenchuk's taxonomy
terms.why_hard: Must be visibly different from 'преставилась' yet equally churchy; do not merge the two rungs

proposed.en: gives up her soul to God

terms.gloss: 'Played into the box', the death-verb Bezenchuk assigns to tall, imposing men like Vorobyaninov
terms.why_hard: Careless choice of 'kicked the bucket' here collides with 'дуба дал' later; the rungs must stay distinct and ranked

terms.gloss: 'Ordered (the rest of us) to live long', a genteel euphemism reserved for former merchant-guild men
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering is opaque; the point is a polite, bourgeois-sounding euphemism, not an order

proposed.ja: 皆に長生きせよと言い残した

terms.gloss: 'Keeled over' or 'stretched out his legs', the coarse rungs for yardmen and peasants
terms.why_hard: Two phrases for the lowest social rank; both must sound rougher than the merchant's and gentleman's phrases

proposed.en: keeled over, or stretched out his legs
proposed.ja: ひっくり返った、または足を伸ばした

terms.gloss: 'Gave the oak', the top rung reserved for the mightiest: railway conductors and bosses; recurs in the book as a catchphrase
terms.why_hard: This one is quoted back later and became a proverb; needs a memorable fixed rendering, not a generic 'died'

proposed.ja: 樫の木をくれてやった

terms.gloss: Low, dismissive death-verb Bezenchuk assigns to himself, 'a small man'
terms.why_hard: Must be the shortest and most contemptuous rung, below even the peasant phrases

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary merchant guilds (first, second guild), abolished by 1917; 'бывший' marks the man as an ex-person
terms.why_hard: The reader needs to see it is an abolished imperial rank, hence the 'former'

terms.gloss: Yard-keeper/house porter, a low urban occupation that recurs throughout the novel (Tikhon later)
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' or 'doorman' misplaces the social station; a fixed word is needed because dvorniks recur

terms.gloss: Glazet, a silver-or-gold-threaded brocade used to line and cover coffins; Bezenchuk's upsell
terms.why_hard: Obsolete trade word; needs a concrete fabric name the reader can picture, and it recurs in the closing line

terms.gloss: Tassels on a coffin's cover, the other item of Bezenchuk's upsell ('с кистями')
terms.why_hard: Ordinary word for brushes/tassels; here it is coffin decoration and pairs with глазет

terms.gloss: Joke Soviet street name: 'Comrade Gubernsky Street', gubernsky meaning 'provincial', mocking renamings after obscure functionaries
terms.why_hard: Translating 'Gubernsky' loses the name; transliterating alone loses the joke; a fixed rendering plus one note

proposed.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

terms.gloss: Central square of Stargorod, a recurring fictional location
terms.why_hard: Recurs across chapters; transliterate consistently, do not translate the 'Old Polish' etymology

proposed.ja: スタロパンスカヤ広場

terms.gloss: Fire-brigade chief, a German loan-title from the imperial service still used in the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Needs a single rendering here and for the firemen's song and Kolka 'брандмейстеров сын'

terms.gloss: The fire chief's name in the drunken song, a pun on насос (pump)
terms.why_hard: Speaking name: transliterate, but the pump joke is lost without a brief note or a rendered nickname

terms.gloss: Horse-drawn fire-brigade train of wagons with a pump and crew, pre-motor era
terms.why_hard: 'Fire engine' is anachronistic; the thin horses and canvas-legged men need a period image

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's 'diamond dreams' of the jewels; a recurring narrator's epithet with the old spelling брильянт
terms.why_hard: Recurs as a leitmotif ('ослепительные мечты' too); keep one fixed phrase across chapters

terms.gloss: Long sheepskin coat worn fur-side in, marker of peasant or tradesman dress
terms.why_hard: Recurs as Bezenchuk's costume; needs one concrete garment word rather than generic 'coat'

terms.gloss: Exasperated concession, 'the devil take you, have it your way'
terms.why_hard: Literal 'devil with you' is meaningless; it must read as a grudging yes

proposed.en: Oh, the devil take you! Go ahead!
proposed.ja: ええい、勝手にしろ！やれ！

conventions: Bezenchuk's ladder of death-verbs is a ranked taxonomy: fix one distinct phrase per rung in each language (преставилась < богу душу отдала < в ящик сыграл < приказал долго жить < перекинулся/ноги протянул < дуба дал, with гигнулся lowest) and reuse the same phrases wherever they recur in the book.

Forms of address are load-bearing: render господин / товарищ / гражданин as three visibly different words in every language (en Mr / Comrade / Citizen; zh 老爷 / 同志 / 公民; ja 旦那 / 同志 / 市民) and keep name-plus-patronymic as one unit, never shortened to a first name.

Russian dialogue dashes become standard quotation marks in en, 「」 in ja and “” in zh; Bezenchuk's rustic particles (значит, ежели, неужто) get a fixed low-colloquial register, while the narrator stays dry and mock-solemn with no added exclamation.

terms.gloss: The young con man protagonist; Ostap Bender, 'the great schemer'
terms.why_hard: Name must be fixed once across all three scripts; ja/zh transliterations of Ostap vary (オスタップ vs オスタプ, 奥斯塔普 vs 奥斯塔卜)

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, now registry-office clerk; the second treasure hunter
terms.why_hard: Narrator alternates 'Ипполит Матвеевич' (name+patronymic, mock-respectful) and 'Воробьянинов'; both forms must be kept distinct and consistent, patronymic not dropped

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Bender's recurring epithet: master of 'combinations', i.e. schemes and swindles
terms.why_hard: Literal 'great combinator' is meaningless in English; 'grand strategist' loses the con-man shade; must be one fixed epithet book-wide

terms.gloss: Petty shopkeeper mentality, penny-pinching (from лавочник, small shopkeeper)
