terms.gloss: a clerk of the voenkomat, the district military commissariat (conscription office)
terms.why_hard: Военкомат is an acronym the reader will meet again; needs a fixed expansion rather than a bare transliteration

terms.gloss: one of the first diners; a surname that comically echoes Bender, the con man introduced later
terms.why_hard: Transliteration should let the echo with 'Bender' survive; do not naturalize the name

terms.gloss: head of the municipal sub-department for urban amenities (roads, parks, monuments)
terms.why_hard: Mock-solemn full bureaucratic title; must sound like an office, and 'благоустройство' is improvement/amenities, not 'well-being'

proposed.en: head of the Municipal Amenities Sub-Department

terms.gloss: the official who demolished the town's only antiquity; surname means 'goat's'
terms.why_hard: Keep as a name; the goat pun is untranslatable and should not be forced

terms.gloss: archaic clerical/church formula 'by whose diligence', parodying inscriptions on buildings and icons
terms.why_hard: The comedy is the pious formula applied to demolition; flat 'thanks to whom' loses the register

proposed.ja: その熱心なる尽力により

terms.gloss: a triumphal arch from the reign of Empress Elizabeth (1741-62), the town's only historic monument
terms.why_hard: 'Elizabethan' in English means Tudor England; the empress must be named

proposed.en: a triumphal arch from the reign of Empress Elizabeth
proposed.zh: 伊丽莎白女皇时代的凯旋门
proposed.ja: エリザヴェータ女帝時代の凱旋門

terms.gloss: a small fur-dressing workshop; 'without a motor' echoes NEP tax and licensing categories that distinguished hand workshops from mechanized ones
terms.why_hard: The deadpan 'без мотора' is a bureaucratic category, not a random detail; keep it as a tag

proposed.zh: 一家小型毛皮加工作坊（无动力）
proposed.ja: 小さな毛皮加工業（動力なし）

terms.gloss: the town consumer cooperative shop, named in Soviet style
terms.why_hard: Shop names in quotation marks need one fixed style; 'Plough and Hammer' should not become 'Hammer and Sickle'

terms.gloss: stocktaking; the standard reason Soviet shops hung a 'closed' sign, here for three weeks
terms.why_hard: The joke is the familiar excuse; render with the stock phrase, not a description

terms.gloss: 'counter workers', Soviet newspaper-speak for shop assistants
terms.why_hard: Parody of official prose; 'shop assistants' loses the register, so keep the officialese

terms.term: двести сорок производителей и не поддающийся учету приплод
terms.gloss: rabbit deaths reported as 'breeding stock' and 'offspring' in the language of a livestock census
terms.why_hard: 'Producers' is wrong; производители here is breeding animals, and the mock-statistical tone must survive

proposed.en: two hundred and forty breeders and an uncountable number of offspring
proposed.zh: 二百四十只种兔和无法统计的幼崽
proposed.ja: 種兎二百四十匹と数え切れぬ仔兎

terms.gloss: biblical phrase 'his spirit rejoiced' (Luke 1:47, Slavonic 'возрадовася дух мой'), used of a priest
terms.why_hard: The scriptural echo is part of the joke; 'cheered up' is too plain

terms.gloss: 'The Sinner's Mirror', a traditional moralizing lubok print and the chapter title
terms.why_hard: Archaic зерцало (mirror) should sound old; the same rendering must serve as chapter title and as picture title

terms.gloss: a Russian popular print, cheap engraved and hand-coloured pictures with moral or comic texts
terms.why_hard: No exact equivalent; keep 'lubok' with a short gloss the first time, then use it bare

terms.gloss: vyaz, the interlaced decorative lettering of Church Slavonic manuscripts and prints
terms.why_hard: Not 'Slavic script' in general; it is the ornamental ligatured style

proposed.ja: 教会スラヴ語の飾り文字

terms.term: «Сим молитву деет, Хам пшеницу сеет, Яфет власть имеет. Смерть всем владеет»
terms.gloss: lubok verse on the three sons of Noah (Shem, Ham, Japheth) as the three estates, with Death ruling all
terms.why_hard: Names must be the standard biblical forms in each language, and the rhymed four-line shape kept

proposed.en: Shem says his prayers, Ham sows the wheat, Japheth holds the power. Death holds sway over all.
proposed.zh: 闪来祈祷，含播麦种，雅弗掌权。死神主宰一切。
proposed.ja: セムは祈り、ハムは麦を蒔き、ヤペテは権を握る。死はすべてを支配す。

terms.gloss: the transience of all earthly things; the memento mori formula
terms.why_hard: Church register; avoid a modern 'everything is temporary'

proposed.en: the vanity of all earthly things
proposed.ja: 地上のすべてのはかなさ

conventions: Dialogue: Russian dash-lines become quoted speech: en double quotes, zh “ ”, ja 「 」; narrator asides stay in the same sentence with commas or dashes, never parenthesized.

Names: en uses simplified BGN-style transliteration without diacritics (Fyodor, Vorobyaninov); zh uses standard Xinhua transliteration; ja uses katakana with ヴ for в; patronymics are kept in all three.

Soviet institutions and acronyms (военкомат, подотдел, кооператив) are expanded into a plain functional title at first occurrence and then reused in that exact form; Japanese uses no honorifics beyond 神父 for отец.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Chapter title and epithet for Alkhen: 'голубой' here means innocent, pure, blushing (the 'sky-blue' colour of naivety), and 'воришка' is a diminutive, half-affectionate 'little thief'
terms.why_hard: A careless translator reads modern 'голубой' as 'gay' or renders it literally as 'blue'; the joke is a bashful, blushing petty thief

terms.gloss: Abbreviation of заведующий хозяйством: the supply/housekeeping manager of a Soviet institution, responsible for stores, furniture and provisions
terms.why_hard: Not a 'housekeeper' or 'janitor'; it is an administrative post that gives access to everything worth stealing, which is the point of the chapter

terms.gloss: The 'Second Home of the Stargorod Social Welfare Department' (Стар[городский] собес = отдел социального обеспечения), an old-women's almshouse housed in Vorobyaninov's former mansion
terms.why_hard: Стар- is Stargorod, not 'old'; собес must be unpacked as a welfare/social-security office; the numbered-institution flavour of Soviet naming should survive

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社会保障处第二养老院
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障局第二養老院

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town ('Old Town') where the novel opens and where Vorobyaninov's mansion stands; hidden inside the acronym Старсобес
terms.why_hard: Should be transliterated, not translated as 'Old Town', and the same form must be used whenever it appears inside acronyms

terms.gloss: The bashful thieving supply manager and director of the almshouse; Альхен is his wife's pet name for him (Germanic diminutive of Alexander)
terms.why_hard: The pet-name pair Альхен/Сашхен must be kept as-is and paired consistently; formal name-and-patronymic must stay name-and-patronymic

proposed.zh: 亚历山大·雅科夫列维奇 / 阿利欣
proposed.ja: アレクサンドル・ヤコヴレヴィチ / アリヘン

terms.gloss: Alkhen's wife, whose name and patronymic mirror his exactly; Сашхен is his pet name for her
terms.why_hard: The comic symmetry of the couple's identical names must be visible in every language; the diminutive endings must match Альхен

proposed.zh: 亚历山德拉·雅科夫列夫娜 / 萨什欣
proposed.ja: アレクサンドラ・ヤコヴレヴナ / サシヘン

terms.gloss: The 'great schemer', the novel's con-man protagonist; here posing as a fire inspector
terms.why_hard: Name must be fixed once for the whole book (Ostap not Ostip; Bender not Bendera), and the established zh/ja forms of published translations should be reused

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, former marshal of the nobility, whose former mansion now houses the almshouse
terms.why_hard: The adjectival form must be re-expressed as 'Vorobyaninov's mansion'; the surname spelling must be locked book-wide

proposed.zh: 沃罗比扬尼诺夫的府邸
proposed.ja: ヴォロビヤニノフの邸宅

terms.gloss: Ostap's mocking nickname for Vorobyaninov: a pun on предводитель дворянства (marshal of the nobility) turned into 'chief of the Comanches'
terms.why_hard: The pun only works if 'marshal of the nobility' has been rendered with a word that can also lead Comanches; recurs in later chapters and must match

terms.gloss: The choir leader (Alkhen); the same word as in предводитель дворянства/команчей, a deliberate echo in the same chapter
terms.why_hard: Translating it as plain 'conductor' loses the echo with 'marshal'; keep the same noun if at all possible

terms.gloss: Bureaucratic formula of the 1920s rationalization campaign: 'in the course of the intensified (compacted) working day', i.e. taking on a second job for the same pay
terms.why_hard: It is a parody of official prose; a bland 'to save time' loses the jargon; needs a rendering that sounds like a Soviet memo

proposed.en: in the spirit of the intensified working day
proposed.zh: 本着紧凑工作日的精神
proposed.ja: 労働日の密度向上の一環として

terms.gloss: The old women housed in the almshouse: called by the absurd official term 'pupils' (воспитанницы, as of a girls' boarding school) and 'pensioners'
terms.why_hard: The comedy is that grey-haired women are officially 'pupils' or 'wards'; render with an equally bureaucratic, slightly wrong noun, consistently

proposed.zh: 院生 / 领养老金的老太太

terms.gloss: The previous director was sacked for rudeness and 'appointed bandmaster of a symphony orchestra': a joke about Soviet cadre reshuffling
terms.why_hard: The old-fashioned German-derived title must sound like a real post so the absurd punishment lands

terms.gloss: Military image: the ragged 'hurrah' of an infantry skirmish line going into attack, heard from a distance
terms.why_hard: 'Chain' is wrong; цепь is a skirmish line; the narrator's WWI/Civil War vocabulary recurs and must be rendered consistently

proposed.en: a distant 'hurrah' along a skirmish line
proposed.zh: 远处散兵线上的'乌拉'声
proposed.ja: 遠くの散兵線から聞こえる「ウラー」

terms.gloss: Ostap's verdict on the mansion: 'vulgar (philistine) luxury'; пошлый is Nabokov's untranslatable 'poshlost'
terms.why_hard: Not 'banal' or 'cheap'; it means tasteless bourgeois ostentation; the word recurs as a narratorial judgement

terms.gloss: Toile-du-nord: cheap coarse cotton cloth, here in mouse grey, the uniform of the almshouse; the name is repeated three times for comic effect
terms.why_hard: Must be kept as a fabric name (not 'cheap cloth') so the triple repetition works; transliterate the same way every time

proposed.zh: 粗棉布(图瓦尔德诺尔布)

terms.gloss: Opening line of the pre-revolutionary romance 'Бубенцы' (lyrics A. Kusikov, music V. Bakaleinikov), a troika-and-snow song the old women sing
terms.why_hard: It is a quoted song, not narration; needs verse layout and a rendering that scans, and a short note that it is a well-known romance

proposed.en: Hear the sleigh-bells ringing from afar
proposed.zh: 远处传来了铃铛的叮当声
proposed.ja: 遠くから鈴の音が聞こえる

terms.gloss: A loose belted Tolstoy blouse, the standard 1920s Soviet office garment, worn by Alkhen
terms.why_hard: Not a modern 'sweatshirt' (the current meaning of толстовка); it must read as a period garment

terms.gloss: Ostap's ironic guess that the choir is doing 'songs of the nationalities', a stock item of Soviet cultural programming
terms.why_hard: The bureaucratic flavour of народности (ethnic minorities) is the joke; 'folk songs' flattens it

terms.gloss: Fire-safety inspector, the identity Ostap assumes to enter the almshouse; his questions about primus stoves follow from it
terms.why_hard: Render as an official title Ostap can wield throughout the chapter, consistent with later mentions

terms.gloss: Standard Soviet form of address, used here by Ostap and Alkhen with mock politeness
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed word in each language and kept even where it sounds stiff; it is period colour

terms.gloss: Primus kerosene stove, the universal cooking device of Soviet communal life and the classic fire hazard
terms.why_hard: Keep the brand-name word; it recurs across the book as an emblem of communal-flat life

terms.term: кружки: хоровой, драматический, изобразительных искусств и музыкальный
terms.gloss: Soviet 'circles' (amateur clubs) that every institution was required to run: choir, drama, fine arts, music
terms.why_hard: кружок is a fixed institutional term, not 'group' or 'class'; the list is a parody of a report and should sound like one

proposed.en: circles: choral, drama, fine arts and music
proposed.zh: 小组:合唱、戏剧、美术和音乐
proposed.ja: サークル:合唱、演劇、美術、音楽

terms.gloss: Brass band (its instruments already sold off by Alkhen); капелла is an old-fashioned word for an ensemble
terms.why_hard: Not 'chapel' or 'choir'; a brass band, so that 'this mass of metal' makes sense

terms.gloss: Harmonium, the reed organ standing in the club room (described as рыжая, reddish-brown)
terms.why_hard: Not 'organ' or 'accordion'; use the standard musical term in each language

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become double quotation marks in English, “…” in Chinese, and 「…」 in Japanese; the narrator's parenthetical asides stay in parentheses in all three.

Names: transliterate surnames and name-plus-patronymic consistently (BGN/PCGN-style in English, established Chinese transliteration, katakana with ・ in Japanese); pet names (Альхен, Сашхен) are transliterated, never translated; товарищ is always comrade / 同志 / 同志.

Quoted songs and verse are set as indented verse lines in all three languages, with a one-line translator's note naming the song on first appearance; Japanese narration uses である体 with 敬体 only inside dialogue.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Colloquial patronymic-only name for Варфоломей Коробейников, the archivist of the Stargorod housing office who sells furniture warrants
terms.why_hard: Patronymic-only address is familiar/half-mocking; rendering it as a surname or first name loses the tone and breaks the link to Коробейников

terms.gloss: Formal Soviet civic address 'citizen' plus the archivist's surname; the narrator uses it with mock officialese
terms.why_hard: 'Citizen' must be kept as the NEP-era neutral form distinct from 'comrade' (тов.), not dropped as Mr.

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the provincial priest who is Vorobyaninov's rival in the chair hunt
terms.why_hard: Must stay one fixed form across the book; 'отец' is the clerical title, not 'father' as parent

terms.gloss: Surname of Father Fyodor, used by the narrator when he wants a dry, secular distance
terms.why_hard: Reader must recognise Востриков and отец Федор as the same man; transliteration must match wherever it recurs

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility whose mother-in-law's chairs hold the jewels
terms.why_hard: A long surname that recurs on every page and in the adjective воробьяниновская; a single transliteration is essential

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility (предводитель дворянства), an elected pre-1917 head of the gentry in a district or province
terms.why_hard: Not a military 'leader'; must map to the recognised English term and to a Chinese/Japanese gloss of the noble rank

terms.gloss: Archivist; Korobeinikov's old-regime job title, which he keeps as a private hoarder of nationalised-furniture records
terms.why_hard: The dated Latinate word is part of the mock-solemn voice; 'clerk' or 'record keeper' flattens it

terms.gloss: A matching set of walnut drawing-room furniture; here the twelve Gambs chairs
terms.why_hard: гарнитур is a 'suite/set', not 'garniture'; гостиный is drawing-room, not 'guest'

proposed.ja: クルミ材の客間用家具セット

terms.gloss: The Gambs firm, Petersburg court furniture makers (Heinrich Gambs and heirs), a quality mark for the twelve chairs
terms.why_hard: Real historical maker; transliteration must be fixed since 'Gambs chairs' is the book's leitmotif

terms.gloss: An official warrant issued by the housing authority allocating a piece of nationalised furniture to a named person
terms.why_hard: Not a purchase 'order' or a military order; it is a distribution document, the plot's paper trail

terms.gloss: Korobeinikov's alphabetical card index of who received what furniture, which he grandly calls 'the mirror of life'; also the chapter title
terms.why_hard: алфавит here is an alphabetical register, not the ABC; the pompous epithet must read as his own phrase

proposed.en: the alphabetical register, 'the Mirror of Life'
proposed.ja: アルファベット索引——「人生の鏡」

terms.gloss: Korobeinikov's back room, mock-named after the Tsarist Secret Chancellery (political police office)
terms.why_hard: A joke on an old-regime institution; 'secret office' alone loses the imperial echo, but a footnote is too heavy

terms.gloss: Madame Popova, wife or widow of a general; the feminine -ша suffix marks status by husband
terms.why_hard: She is not herself a general; rendering must carry 'general's wife/widow' compactly

terms.gloss: Comrade Bruns, the engineer to whom a warrant for the twelve walnut chairs was issued; a recurring quarry of Father Fyodor
terms.why_hard: тов. is the standard abbreviation of товарищ; keep the Soviet 'Comrade' rather than expanding to Mr.

terms.gloss: Street address (Vinogradnaya Street 34) on the warrant, in Stargorod
terms.why_hard: Street name means 'Vine/Grape Street'; transliterate, do not translate, and keep the Russian address order convention

proposed.ja: ヴィノグラードナヤ通り34番地

terms.gloss: Tsarist gold ten-rouble coins, hoarded illegally and traded at a premium against Soviet paper roubles in the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Not 'tens' of money; the reader needs to grasp these are pre-revolutionary gold coins with black-market value

proposed.ja: 帝政期の十ルーブル金貨

terms.term: По курсу приму. По девять с половиной
terms.gloss: Korobeinikov accepts gold at the day's unofficial rate: 9.5 Soviet roubles per gold ten
terms.why_hard: The joke is that a Soviet archivist quotes a black-market exchange rate like a banker; the figures must stay intelligible

proposed.en: I'll take them at the rate. Nine and a half. Today's rate.
proposed.zh: 按牌价收。九块半。今天的牌价。
proposed.ja: 相場で受け取ります。九ルーブル半。今日の相場です。

terms.gloss: Slang for gold coins, literally 'yellow ones'
terms.why_hard: A colloquial coinage; needs an equally informal but transparent rendering, not 'gold coins' twice

terms.gloss: Two roubles fifty in silver coin (полтина = fifty kopecks)
terms.why_hard: полтина is not 'half' in the abstract; careless rendering gives wrong arithmetic (5×9.5 + 2.5 = 50)

proposed.en: two and a half in silver

terms.gloss: The sausage-shaped roll of gold coins Father Fyodor had sewn into his jacket lining
terms.why_hard: Literal 'little sausage' with no context confuses; the image of a coin roll must be kept without explaining it away

proposed.ja: ソーセージ状に巻いた金貨

terms.gloss: 'You'll lick your fingers' — it is delicious/first-rate, a salesman's patter about the furniture
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering is odd in English; the target idiom should stay a food metaphor for the comic mismatch with chairs

proposed.ja: 指までなめたくなりますよ

terms.gloss: Duped, made a fool of (from колпак, a fool's cap)
terms.why_hard: Register is street-comic; 'deceived' is too flat

proposed.zh: 被他耍得团团转的买主
proposed.ja: まんまとカモにした買い手

terms.gloss: Practical shrewdness, quick-wittedness in getting one's way
terms.why_hard: A folksy noun; 'intelligence' misses the sly, mercantile connotation

terms.gloss: Heavy woollen overcoat cloth; the archivist judges the visitor's means by touch in the dark
terms.why_hard: Not 'drape'; the material name signals a respectable coat in a comic aside

terms.gloss: Said a perfunctory prayer; Soviet orthography prints бог in lower case
terms.why_hard: Translators must decide once whether 'God' is capitalised in the target; the character's rote piety is the joke

proposed.en: said an absent-minded prayer to God
proposed.zh: 心不在焉地向上帝祷告

conventions: Dialogue introduced by the Russian em dash is rendered with the target language's standard quotation marks (en: double quotes; zh: “”; ja: 「」), one speaker per paragraph, never reproducing the dash.
Soviet forms of address are kept and fixed: гражданин/гражданка = Citizen/公民/市民, товарищ/тов. = Comrade/同志/同志; отец before a priest's name = Father/神父/神父 (as a suffix in zh and ja).

Personal names are transliterated once per language and reused verbatim, including patronymic-only forms (Варфоломеич) and adjectival derivatives (воробьяниновская мебель = Vorobyaninov's furniture); the trailing Wikisource line 'Категория:…' is a scraping artefact and is omitted.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the perpetually idle 'locksmith-intellectual' of Stargorod, always carrying a can; a recurring character
terms.why_hard: Narrator names him by name-and-patronymic throughout; dropping the patronymic loses the mock-respectful tone, and the same person is also 'Витька-слесарь' in the yard-keeper's mouth

proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ

terms.gloss: The yard-keeper's contemptuous diminutive for Polesov: 'Vitka the locksmith'
terms.why_hard: Diminutive must read as familiar-contemptuous, not affectionate; keep the link to Viktor Mikhailovich visible to a reader unused to Russian name forms

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, the fortune-teller (гадалка), Vorobyaninov's former flame; recurring character
terms.why_hard: Also referred to simply as 'гадалка'; both designations must map to one person consistently; Polish patronymic must not be russified in zh/ja

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: Fortune-teller (cards, parrot); a semi-legal NEP-era trade practised by fallen gentlewomen
terms.why_hard: Must be the same word every time as it is her narrative label (and in the chapter title); avoid 'witch'/'psychic' connotations

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, former marshal of the nobility, the protagonist; here recognised despite having shaved his moustache
terms.why_hard: Spelling must be fixed book-wide; zh/ja have several competing transliterations in existing translations

terms.gloss: House yard-keeper: sweeps, locks the gate, and traditionally acts as informal police auxiliary and eyes of the building
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor'/'caretaker' loses the street authority and the tsarist-era policing role that makes his rage and arrest funny; must be one term book-wide

terms.gloss: Metal fitter / locksmith-mechanic; Polesov's trade and his self-important self-designation 'слесарь-механик'
terms.why_hard: 'Locksmith' alone is too narrow, 'mechanic' too grand; the yard-keeper spits 'слесарь-механик' as an insult about pretension, so the rendering must sound both technical and puffed-up

proposed.zh: 修锁匠 / 机械修锁匠
proposed.ja: 錠前屋 / 錠前機械工

terms.gloss: A metal milk can with lid; Polesov's constant, absurd prop (he never fills it)
terms.why_hard: Not a 'bucket' or 'jerry-can'; it is a recurring comic object and the same word must be used every time it appears

terms.gloss: Repair of Primus kerosene pressure stoves, the ubiquitous 1920s cooking appliance
terms.why_hard: The sign is quoted verbatim twice and carried off as evidence; 'Primus' should stay as a brand word, with the stove type made explicit for zh/ja readers

proposed.ja: プリムス・コンロ修理

terms.term: Ход в слесарную мастерскую / Слесарная мастерская и починка примусов
terms.gloss: The two painted shop signs at Polesov's never-open workshop
terms.why_hard: Set as display text; must be typographically distinct (centered/small caps) and identical wherever the sign reappears

proposed.en: ENTRANCE TO LOCKSMITH'S WORKSHOP / LOCKSMITH'S WORKSHOP AND PRIMUS STOVE REPAIRS
proposed.zh: 修锁作坊入口 / 修锁作坊 兼修普里姆斯煤油炉
proposed.ja: 錠前工房入口 / 錠前工房 ならびにプリムス・コンロ修理

terms.gloss: Fictional Soviet packing cooperative ('quick-pack'), a typical NEP portmanteau acronym; its lads help drag the yard-keeper away
terms.why_hard: A comic made-up acronym; transliterating ('Bystroupak') kills the joke, so it should be built as an equally clunky compound in each target

terms.gloss: Officer of the Soviet 'militsiya', i.e. the ordinary police
terms.why_hard: 'Militiaman' misleads English readers into thinking paramilitary; but 'policeman' erases the Soviet flavour; choose once for the whole book

terms.gloss: The local (district) police station; both words denote the same destination here
terms.why_hard: Two Russian words for one place on the same page; render both as 'the station' rather than inventing two locations

terms.gloss: 'Gangrene' as a personal insult, the yard-keeper's favourite epithet for Polesov
terms.why_hard: Should stay literal and absurd (it is funny because it is a medical word) rather than being normalised to a standard curse

terms.gloss: Folk insult: 'seven-fathered viper', i.e. a bastard viper of unknown paternity; then echoed by the narrator with deadpan literalness
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered so that the narrator's later repetition ('the seven-fathered viper with a secondary education') remains verbatim and funny

terms.gloss: Secondary (gymnasium-level) education, thrown at Polesov as proof he is a pretentious 'educated' parasite
terms.why_hard: Class marker: in 1927 having finished secondary school set one apart from the yard-keeper; 'high school diploma' flattens this; also recurs in the narrator's echo

terms.gloss: 'Dog of an aristocrat' — a class-hatred insult (собачий = 'damned, doggy')
terms.why_hard: Should keep 'aristocrat' as the operative political sneer of the era rather than becoming a generic 'snob'

terms.gloss: Boor, lout; the standard word with which the pre-revolutionary educated class dismissed the lower orders — Polesov's counter-insult
terms.why_hard: Recurs across the book (Vorobyaninov, Polesov); must consistently sound like an offended gentleman's word, not street abuse

terms.gloss: Narrator's mock-solemn label for the yard-keeper's printable words, as against the unprintable ones he prefers
terms.why_hard: Keep the ironic euphemism ('parliamentary language') rather than paraphrasing it away as 'polite words'

terms.gloss: 'The weak female estate' — narrator's parody of tsarist estate (сословие) terminology applied to the women at the windows
terms.why_hard: Сословие is the legal term for social estate; translate with a bureaucratic-legal word so the mock-solemnity survives

terms.gloss: The Bolsheviks, i.e. the ruling party; used by the 'former people' with hostile irony
terms.why_hard: Standard rendering, but tone: in Polesov's mouth it is an enemy's name, not a neutral political label

terms.gloss: The ten years since October 1917, dating the action to 1927
terms.why_hard: Should not be rounded or made vague; it anchors the book's chronology and Polesov's accumulated irony

terms.gloss: 'Nobody shaves off a moustache for nothing' — Polesov's aphorism that became proverbial
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a proverb, short and quotable, since it is one of the novel's remembered lines

proposed.en: Nobody shaves off a moustache for nothing.
proposed.ja: 髭を剃るのには理由があるものだ。

terms.gloss: Kompot, stewed fruit in syrup, served in a saucer as a modest treat
terms.why_hard: Not 'compote' in the Western jam sense and not 'juice'; a household staple across the book

proposed.ja: コンポート（果物の砂糖煮）

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become English double quotes, Chinese “…” and Japanese 「…」; keep one utterance per line as in the original.
Polesov and Elena Stanislavovna address each other with вы plus name-and-patronymic: render as polite register (Japanese です/ます, Chinese 您), and never anglicise or shorten patronymics.

Fictional Soviet acronyms (Быстроупак etc.) are rendered as invented compounds in each target language, not transliterated; real institutions (милиция) get one fixed rendering with a translator's note on first occurrence only.

terms.gloss: Chapter title; Ostap's fake monarchist cell, a pun on Isaiah's 'swords into ploughshares' (орало = archaic 'plough', also sounds like орать 'to bawl')
terms.why_hard: Rendering 'орало' as a modern word loses both the biblical echo and the mock-archaic pomposity; must stay fixed as an organisation name across many chapters

proposed.en: The Union of the Sword and Ploughshare

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the con man; the narrator alternates his name with the epithet 'великий комбинатор'
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Ostap, not Ostap/Ostup); zh/ja readers need one stable form

terms.gloss: The narrator's standing epithet for Ostap Bender, the 'grand schemer'
terms.why_hard: Not a job; a mock-heroic title used dozens of times, must be one fixed phrase, not paraphrased anew each time

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, former marshal of the nobility; narrator switches between first-name-patronymic and surname
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must not be dropped or turned into a surname; zh/ja transliterations are long and must be consistent

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 / 沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ / ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna, fortune-teller, Vorobyaninov's mistress before 1917
terms.why_hard: Polish-flavoured patronymic; narrator also calls her 'старуха' and 'гадалка', all three must map to one character

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the hyperactive mechanic-locksmith and would-be monarchist
terms.why_hard: Addressed by name-patronymic in dialogue, by surname in narration; the narrator also calls him 'слесарь' and 'кустарь-одиночка с мотором'

proposed.zh: 波列索夫 / 维克托·米哈伊洛维奇
proposed.ja: ポレソフ / ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ

terms.gloss: Polesov's trade: a metal-fitter/locksmith who repairs anything mechanical
terms.why_hard: 'Locksmith' alone is too narrow; 'mechanic' loses the artisan flavour; must match whatever is used for him elsewhere

terms.gloss: NEP-era tax/licence category: an independent artisan working alone with a motor, taxed above a hand craftsman; Polesov's recurring official label
terms.why_hard: A bureaucratic classification used as a comic epithet; a literal 'lone craftsman with a motor' reads as nonsense without signalling it is officialese

proposed.en: a one-man motorised artisan (his official tax category)
proposed.zh: 带电动机的个体手工业者
proposed.ja: モーター付き個人手工業者

terms.gloss: Fortune-teller (cards, palms); Elena Stanislavovna's NEP livelihood
terms.why_hard: Should be a plain noun ('the fortune-teller'), not 'witch' or 'psychic'; used by narrator as her label

terms.gloss: A girl pupil of a pre-revolutionary gymnasium (classical secondary school)
terms.why_hard: 'Schoolgirl' erases the class marker; 'gymnast' is a false friend

terms.gloss: The Paris Exposition Universelle of 1900; 'ninety-nine' dates their affair to the eve of it
terms.why_hard: Reader must recognise a dated world's fair, not a generic exhibition; year 1899 must be kept as the characters say it

terms.gloss: 'Magnanimous knight': the old woman's sentimental epithet for Vorobyaninov
terms.why_hard: Mock-romantic register from pre-revolutionary novels; must sound faded, not sincere

proposed.ja: あの寛大な騎士のまま

terms.gloss: The Stargorod lane whose gate Polesov dismantled and never repaired; a running gag
terms.why_hard: Street name must be transliterated identically every time; the gate fragment is a callback readers must recognise

proposed.ja: ペレレシン横丁五番地

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary municipal executive board elected by the town duma; Vorobyaninov reminisces about its elections
terms.why_hard: Not a Soviet body; 'city council' alone hides that this is old-regime politics

terms.gloss: 'Lowering his voice to the level of complete illegality': parody of revolutionary-underground conspiracy language
terms.why_hard: The joke is that Ostap performs a clandestine cell; a flat 'whisper' loses the mockery of political-underground jargon

proposed.en: lowering his voice to a pitch of total illegality
proposed.zh: 把嗓音压低到彻底非法的程度
proposed.ja: 声を完全に非合法な低さに落として

terms.gloss: Ostap's question and Polesov's absurd answer; became a Russian proverb for empty enthusiasm
terms.why_hard: Must stay literally absurd ('Always!'), not smoothed into a sensible reply; readers of the whole book see it echoed

terms.gloss: Supporter of Grand Duke Kirill Vladimirovich, who proclaimed himself Emperor in exile in 1924; an émigré monarchist faction
terms.why_hard: Meaningless without the name; needs an in-text expansion once, then a fixed short form

proposed.en: a Kirillite (a supporter of Grand Duke Kirill's claim to the throne)

terms.gloss: Military regulation affirmative, 'Yes, sir!'
terms.why_hard: A civilian 'exactly' misses that Polesov snaps to attention; must be the same barracks formula every time

proposed.ja: はっ、その通りであります！

terms.gloss: White/monarchist pathos formula Ostap barks at Polesov; recurs as his cell's slogan
terms.why_hard: Should be rendered as a set slogan, capital-R Russia, identical each recurrence

proposed.ja: ロシアは君を忘れない！

terms.gloss: Formula of imperial decrees ('has been graciously pleased to command') that surfaces in Ostap's head
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a fossilised chancery phrase, not ordinary speech; English has a real equivalent formula

terms.gloss: 'Above-average blackmail': narrator's deadpan bureaucratic grading of Ostap's coming swindle
terms.why_hard: The comedy is the statistical adjective; do not normalise to 'big' or 'serious'

terms.gloss: Samovar, the tea urn; here carried in as the signal that supper begins
terms.why_hard: Keep as loanword in all three languages; do not turn into 'kettle' or 'teapot'

terms.gloss: Ostap's mock-gallant French address to Elena Stanislavovna
terms.why_hard: Must stay 'Madame', signalling émigré/pre-revolutionary posture, not a neutral 'Ma'am'

terms.gloss: 'The old woman': narrator's blunt label for Elena Stanislavovna in the same scene where she is a former beauty
terms.why_hard: Softening to 'the elderly lady' kills the deadpan cruelty; pick one word and keep it

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become double quotes in en, “ ” in zh, 「 」 in ja; keep one exchange per line as in the original.
Names: name + patronymic kept in full in all languages (en transliteration fixed once, zh 中点 between elements, ja ・ between elements); never replace with a surname or first name alone.

Register: the old lovers and all conspirators use вы, so ja dialogue stays in です/ます with 敬語 and zh uses 您; narrator's fixed epithets (великий комбинатор, старуха, слесарь) are rendered by one fixed phrase each, book-wide.

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's first name and patronymic; the narrator's habitual way of naming him
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must not be dropped or turned into a surname; one fixed transliteration for the whole book

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Surname of the former marshal of the nobility, the co-hero
terms.why_hard: Alternates with Ипполит Матвеевич for the same man; readers must recognise both as one person

terms.gloss: The 'great schemer', a young con man who becomes Vorobyaninov's partner

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's late mother-in-law, who hid the jewels in a chair
terms.why_hard: Referred to both by name and as тёща; the reader must link the two

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: Wife's mother specifically (Russian distinguishes from husband's mother)
terms.why_hard: English flattens to 'mother-in-law'; zh and ja must consistently pick the wife's-mother term

terms.gloss: Ostap's catchphrase: 'things are moving at last', mock-addressed to a jury
terms.why_hard: Became a proverb; must be rendered identically every time it recurs, keeping the courtroom parody

proposed.en: The ice is breaking, gentlemen of the jury!

proposed.ja: 氷が動き出しましたよ、陪審員の皆さん！

terms.gloss: Ostap's second courtroom catchphrase, 'the session continues', meaning 'back to business'
terms.why_hard: Recurs throughout the book and in Russian usage; needs one fixed rendering matching the jury phrase

terms.term: ключ от квартиры, где деньги лежат
terms.gloss: 'The key to the apartment where the money is' — Ostap's sarcasm for an absurdly greedy demand
terms.why_hard: Proverbial in Russian; literal rendering is fine but must stay word-for-word stable across recurrences

proposed.en: the key to the apartment where the money is kept
proposed.ja: 金の置いてあるアパートの鍵

terms.gloss: Ostap's mocking epithet for Vorobyaninov, riffing on his cover story of being an émigré returned from Paris
terms.why_hard: Ironic 'comrade' plus bourgeois Paris; must keep Soviet word 'comrade', not 'friend'

proposed.ja: 親愛なるパリからの同志

terms.gloss: Ostap's joke: 'before the era of historical materialism' = before the Revolution
terms.why_hard: Marxist jargon used as a comic periodisation; must stay literal so the joke lands, not 'before the revolution'

proposed.en: before the era of historical materialism
proposed.zh: 历史唯物主义时代以前
proposed.ja: 史的唯物論の時代以前

terms.gloss: NEP-era concession: a licence granted to private (often foreign) capital to run an enterprise; Ostap's ironic name for the treasure hunt
terms.why_hard: Recurring running joke (концессионеры); needs a business-legal word, not 'partnership'

proposed.ja: コンセッション（利権事業）

terms.gloss: 'Technical director of the enterprise' — Soviet managerial title Ostap assigns himself
terms.why_hard: Bureaucratic title used comically; keep stiff official register

proposed.zh: 本项事业的技术负责人

terms.gloss: Acronym for social insurance (социальное страхование), employer contributions under Soviet labour law
terms.why_hard: Acronym opaque to target readers; render as the concept, not a transliteration

terms.gloss: The yardkeeper's (дворник's) lodge, here the setting of the pact between Ostap and Vorobyaninov
terms.why_hard: No exact Western equivalent; 'janitor's room' loses the Russian courtyard-porter institution

terms.gloss: A beaver-felt hat, pre-revolutionary gentleman's headgear
terms.why_hard: Not 'castor oil'; a marker of Vorobyaninov's faded gentility

proposed.ja: ビーバーのフェルト帽

terms.gloss: Pince-nez, Vorobyaninov's constant prop
terms.why_hard: Recurs constantly; fix one word rather than alternating glasses/spectacles

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary land unit, about 1.09 hectares; 'a fermoir that cost the harvest of 500 desyatinas'
terms.why_hard: Converting to hectares kills the period flavour; transliterate with the unit kept recognisable

terms.gloss: French 'fermoir': a jewelled clasp worn as a short necklace
terms.why_hard: Not a generic 'clasp'; it is a piece of jewellery in its own right

proposed.ja: 宝石付きフェルモワール（首飾りの留め金）

terms.gloss: Andy Tucker, the con man in O. Henry's 'The Gentle Grafter', whom Ostap quotes as an authority
terms.why_hard: Reader may not know the reference; keep the name and gloss lightly ('O. Henry's Andy Tucker') if allowed

proposed.zh: 安迪·塔克（欧·亨利笔下的骗子）
proposed.ja: アンディ・タッカー（O・ヘンリーの詐欺師）

terms.gloss: Rogue, swindler; the narrator's tag for Ostap on first meeting
terms.why_hard: Register is colloquial-contemptuous but affectionate; not 'criminal'

terms.gloss: Narrator's mock-epic epithet 'the magnificent Ostap'
terms.why_hard: Part of a family of Homeric epithets for Ostap; keep one fixed adjective

terms.gloss: Chapter title: the 'diamond haze' of the jewel vision that fills the lodge
terms.why_hard: Chapter-title image echoed in the text (дым держался под потолком); the same word must be used both places

terms.gloss: 'Robbery in broad daylight' — Vorobyaninov's protest at Ostap's 60 percent
terms.why_hard: Has direct idiomatic equivalents; do not translate word by word

terms.gloss: Odessa-flavoured slang: 'this whole outfit/business', here of the jewels
terms.why_hard: Literal 'music' is nonsense; a colloquial catch-all is needed

terms.gloss: A matched drawing-room furniture suite, here the twelve chairs themselves
terms.why_hard: The object of the whole novel; fix one phrase and reuse it every time the set is named

conventions: Ostap's recurring catchphrases (Лед тронулся…, Заседание продолжается, ключ от квартиры…) are rendered once and reused verbatim in all three languages wherever they recur.
Russian dialogue dashes become quotation marks: en "…", zh “…”, ja 「…」; the вы between Ostap and Vorobyaninov is kept as formal register (ja です/ます, Ostap's mock-solemn politeness preserved).
Names are transliterated once for the whole book with patronymics kept (en BGN-style, zh standard 新华社 transliteration, ja katakana with long-vowel marks) and never localised.

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man and co-protagonist; the narrator calls him simply Остап
terms.why_hard: Name must be transliterated identically book-wide; zh/ja phonetic forms vary widely and must be fixed once

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility; here Ostap poses as his son ('молодой Воробьянинов')
terms.why_hard: The irony of 'young Vorobyaninov' for Ostap is lost if the reader cannot recognise the fixed surname form

terms.gloss: Ostap's improvised alias: the Frenchified 'Voldemar', which the archivist instantly normalises to the Russian name + patronymic from Ippolit
terms.why_hard: The joke is that Ostap gives a pretentious name and the old man supplies the patronymic; keep both forms and the patronymic mechanism visible (ja/zh readers need a consistent patronymic scheme)

proposed.zh: 沃尔德马尔／弗拉基米尔·伊波利托维奇
proposed.ja: ヴォルデマール／ウラジーミル・イッポリトヴィチ

terms.gloss: Varfolomei Korobeinikov, the retired archivist who hoards the furniture-allocation warrants at home
terms.why_hard: Surname derives from коробейник (pedlar) — do not translate it; transliterate consistently with later chapters

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, Vorobyaninov's old flame, now a fortune-teller in Stargorod
terms.why_hard: Ostap has just claimed she is dead; the narrator's aside that the archivist saw her at the meat stalls today is the joke — name form must match her earlier chapters

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: Archivist — the old man's former post in the communal-housing office; the narrator uses it as his fixed epithet
terms.why_hard: Dated, faintly Tsarist-clerical word; 'archivist' is fine but must be used as a recurring epithet, not varied with 'clerk'

terms.gloss: Abbreviation of коммунальное хозяйство: the local Communal Services (housing) department that requisitioned and redistributed furniture after the Revolution
terms.why_hard: A Soviet acronym; a bare transliteration is opaque, a long paraphrase kills the rhythm — needs one short fixed rendering

terms.gloss: An official warrant/voucher by which confiscated furniture was allocated to a person or institution; the plot's paper trail
terms.why_hard: 'Order' in English suggests a command or a purchase order; the sense is an allocation warrant. Recurs throughout the book

terms.gloss: Commercial formula 'cash against documents', applied by Ostap to buying the warrants
terms.why_hard: Must echo trade jargon, not read as a literal preposition; ties to the fixed rendering of ордер

proposed.ja: 証書と引き換えに現金で

terms.why_hard: Sounds like 'freelancer' but was an official bureaucratic class; keep the bureaucratic flavour

terms.gloss: A 'refrigerated slaughterhouse on a cooperative (artel) basis' — Ostap's invented NEP business; артель is a workers' cooperative
terms.why_hard: The comedy is the pompous Soviet compound noun plus the cooperative buzzword; a flat 'meat-packing plant' loses it

proposed.en: a refrigerated slaughterhouse run on cooperative lines
proposed.zh: 合作社性质的冷藏屠宰场
proposed.ja: 協同組合方式の冷凍屠畜場

terms.term: Ближе к телу, как говорит Мопассан
terms.gloss: Ostap twists the idiom ближе к делу ('get to the point') into ближе к телу ('closer to the body') and credits it to Maupassant as mock erudition
terms.why_hard: A pun plus a fake attribution; a literal rendering is nonsense. Needs a target-language pun on 'get to the point' or a note

proposed.en: Let's get down to bodies, as Maupassant says.
proposed.zh: 言归正传——不，言归正床，莫泊桑说的。
proposed.ja: モーパッサンいわく、話を本題に、いや本体に戻しましょう。

terms.gloss: 'Is oats expensive these days?' — the stock excuse of cabmen for high fares, used ironically about the archivist's price
terms.why_hard: Culturally specific cabman joke; literal 'oats' baffles unless the cabman frame is signalled

proposed.en: Has the price of oats gone up, cabbie?
proposed.ja: 近ごろ馬の燕麦が値上がりでもしたのかね？

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary servile formula 'you are pleased to jest', marking the archivist as an Old Regime clerk
terms.why_hard: Register: obsequious, dated; a modern 'you're joking' loses the class marker

proposed.en: You are pleased to jest, sir…

terms.why_hard: Post-1917 'господа' is politically loaded (ex-masters); 'gentlemen' alone misses that he is betting on a restoration

terms.gloss: 'Hero of Labour', an honorary Soviet title instituted 1927; Ostap applies it mockingly to the hoarding clerk
terms.why_hard: Should match the official title's fixed rendering, capitalised, to keep the mock-official tone

proposed.ja: まさに労働英雄ですね

terms.gloss: 'Full mechanisation' — 1920s industrial slogan, applied by Ostap to a shelf with pasted letters
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a slogan of the period, not a technical description

terms.gloss: 'Green armour' — the narrator's recurring epithet for Ostap's tight green suit
terms.why_hard: Recurring image; render 'armour' literally each time rather than normalising to 'suit'

terms.gloss: Familiar 'pops/old man' — Ostap's mock-affectionate address to older men, also used for his 'late father'
terms.why_hard: Ostap uses it both for his fictional father and as cheeky address to Korobeinikov on the same page; keep one rendering for the vocative

terms.gloss: Non-standard plural of мебель (uneducated/petty-bourgeois speech) in the archivist's monologue
terms.why_hard: Marks the speaker's class; a flat 'furniture' erases it — needs a colloquial deviation

terms.gloss: 'Go look for the wind in the field' — a wild-goose chase
terms.why_hard: Proverb; choose an equivalent idiom, not a calque

terms.gloss: 'We live on a volcano' — the archivist's hint that the Soviet order may collapse any day
terms.why_hard: Must stay a cautious hint, not explicit anti-Soviet talk

proposed.en: We're living on a volcano, you know
proposed.zh: 咱们就跟坐在火山口上一样
proposed.ja: わしらは火山の上に住んでいるようなものでして

terms.gloss: Samara, Volga city, the site of Ostap's fictitious slaughterhouse
terms.why_hard: Fixed transliteration; not to be updated to Soviet-era 'Kuibyshev'

terms.gloss: 'Scum/swine' — Ostap's blunt private verdict on Korobeinikov ('a typical bastard')
terms.why_hard: Register: coarse but not obscene; keep the same rendering wherever Ostap uses it

conventions: Dialogue keeps the Russian em-dash convention in en (— …) and uses the standard quotation marks of zh (“ ”) and ja (「 」); narrator's asides that undercut speakers (e.g. 'though he had seen her at the market that very day') stay as plain deadpan sentences, never in parentheses.

Name + patronymic is kept in full (Vladimir Ippolitovich; 弗拉基米尔·伊波利托维奇; ウラジーミル・イッポリトヴィチ) with one fixed transliteration table for all three languages; no honorific suffix (-さん) is added in ja except where the Russian itself is formal (вы + patronymic).

Soviet acronyms (Коммунхоз etc.) get one short expanded rendering per language on every occurrence, never a bare transliteration and never a footnote; NEP realia (артель, ордер, свободная профессия) are rendered by fixed glossary terms.

terms.gloss: Orthodox monk who has taken the strictest monastic vows (the 'great schema'), living as a recluse

terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Evpl/Yevpl); the deliberately odd sound should survive, not be normalised to a familiar name

terms.gloss: Elevated/ecclesiastical word for a monastery

terms.gloss: Here in the religious sense: an ascetic feat, a spiritual exploit (подвижник = ascetic)
terms.why_hard: Modern sense 'heroic deed' misleads; the hagiographic sense is the joke, since the feat is lying in a coffin eating rusks

terms.gloss: An ascetic, one who performs spiritual exploits; synonym set with схимник, отшельник, старец, молчальник
terms.why_hard: Five near-synonyms for one man; rendering each with a different unrelated word confuses, rendering all identically flattens the mock-liturgical variation

terms.gloss: A venerated holy elder (spiritual father), not merely 'old man'; contrasted on the page with the plain старик (peasant)
terms.why_hard: Both старец and старик are 'old man' in English; the text plays them against each other, so they need two distinct fixed renderings

terms.gloss: One under a vow of silence; hagiographic epithet, comic when his first words in 25 years are a request for kerosene
terms.why_hard: Needs to sound like a saint's title, not a description

terms.gloss: Dried bread / rusks, the classic ascetic's and prisoner's ration
terms.why_hard: 'Crackers' or 'biscuits' sound like snacks; the poverty/penance connotation matters

terms.gloss: Bast (birch-bark) shoes, the emblem of the poor Russian peasant
terms.why_hard: Marks the visitor instantly as a peasant; 'sandals' or 'shoes' loses that; needs a fixed compact rendering wherever peasants appear in the book

terms.gloss: The Bolsheviks; here as reported by the peasant, the outside history reaching the cave
terms.why_hard: Trivial in English, but Chinese/Japanese have several established forms; fix one for the book

terms.gloss: Sovkhoz, a state-owned farm (as opposed to a kolkhoz collective); monasteries were commonly converted into them
terms.why_hard: Must not be confused with kolkhoz/collective farm; 'state farm' is understandable without a note

terms.gloss: The coffin the hermit sleeps in as a bed (an actual ascetic practice), later called 'his gloomy bed'
terms.why_hard: Keep it literally 'coffin' throughout; softening to 'casket' or 'bed' kills the bedbug joke

terms.gloss: A dugout, an earth-covered hut half below ground
terms.why_hard: 'Cave' or 'cabin' is wrong; it is a man-made earth dwelling

terms.gloss: Riding breeches flared at the thigh (from Gen. Galliffet), the uniform look of 1920s Soviet military/security men
terms.why_hard: Together with spurs and Mausers it codes the visitors as Chekists/Red commanders without saying so; 'trousers' loses the signal

proposed.ja: だぶだぶの乗馬ズボン

terms.gloss: Mauser C96 pistols in their wooden holster-stocks, iconic sidearm of Civil-War commissars and the Cheka/GPU
terms.why_hard: 'Boxes' is literal but odd; the reader must understand these are holsters and that the men are the security police

proposed.zh: 装在光亮木盒里的毛瑟手枪
proposed.ja: 磨かれた木製ホルスターに収めたモーゼル拳銃

terms.gloss: Bedbugs described as cherry-coloured (engorged with blood)
terms.why_hard: 'Cherry' must read as colour, not fruit; bedbugs (клопы) recur in the book (Bender's boarding-house world) and need one fixed word

terms.gloss: Kerosene, the universal Soviet household fuel and folk pesticide
terms.why_hard: US 'kerosene' vs UK 'paraffin'; fix one for the whole book (kerosene stoves, primus lamps recur)

terms.gloss: A branded bedbug powder of the NEP years, named after Mount Aragats in Armenia; an intrusion of consumer advertising into a saint's life
terms.why_hard: Should keep the brand name and quotes, with 'bedbug powder' spelled out; a translator might drop the name or explain it in a footnote it does not need

proposed.ja: 南京虫駆除粉「アラガツ」

terms.gloss: A thin resinous wood splinter burned for light in peasant huts
terms.why_hard: 'Torch' is too grand, 'match' too small; a 'burning splinter' is the peasant remedy the text means

terms.gloss: Parody of the heroic Civil-War/Red-Army formula 'we die but do not surrender', applied to bedbugs
terms.why_hard: Must keep the military-communiqué ring so the parody lands; a colloquial 'the bugs kept coming' loses it

proposed.en: The bedbugs died, but did not surrender.
proposed.ja: 南京虫は死んでいったが、降伏はしなかった。

terms.gloss: The ascetic practice of fasting (twenty-five years of it)
terms.why_hard: 'Fasting' alone sounds like a diet; the religious-discipline sense should stay

terms.gloss: Recurring mock-solemn formula for the hermit's 'comprehension of life', repeated in escalating variants until the bedbugs arrive
terms.why_hard: The repetition is the joke; each recurrence should use the same fixed phrase rather than elegant variation

proposed.en: knowledge of life / had comprehended life
proposed.zh: 对生活的领悟 / 领悟了生活
proposed.ja: 人生の悟り / 人生を悟った

conventions: The hermit parable is written as a straight-faced parody of a saint's Life: keep the hagiographic register (ascetic feat, holy elder, brethren, ascetic fasting) consistently and never signal the joke with colloquialisms; let the kerosene and bedbug powder do the work.
Fix one rendering per member of the synonym set схимник / отшельник / подвижник / старец / молчальник and reuse it book-wide; keep старец (holy elder) and старик (old man) visibly distinct.

Soviet institutional terms (совхоз, later колхоз, губисполком etc.) are rendered by a short understandable English/Chinese/Japanese equivalent, with the transliterated Russian in parentheses only on first occurrence in the book, never as a footnote.

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the con man and 'great schemer', co-protagonist

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, co-protagonist; here his late father is meant

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫

proposed.ja: コロベイニコフ（文書保管人）

terms.why_hard: It is a nickname (from Alexander), needs one fixed spelling in each language

terms.gloss: Disabled war veteran who received one chair; his widow later marries Bender

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary merchant rank (First Guild = richest class of merchants)

terms.gloss: Head of the chancellery of the pre-revolutionary town council

proposed.en: chief clerk of the Town Board

terms.gloss: City military commissariat (draft and military-affairs office)
terms.why_hard: Acronym should be expanded, not transliterated; not a person ('commissar') but an office

terms.gloss: Parodic acronym: Stargorod Provincial Food Committee (NEP-era supply body)
terms.why_hard: The joke is the monstrous acronym itself; keep a transliteration plus a short expansion, do not silently expand only

proposed.zh: "斯省粮委"（斯塔尔戈罗德省粮食委员会）
proposed.ja: スタルプロドコムグブ（スタルゴロド県食糧委員会）

terms.gloss: Social security department; its '2nd Home' is the old people's home Alkhen runs
terms.why_hard: Must match the rendering used in chapter 8; 'дом собеса' is an almshouse, not an office building

proposed.en: Social Security / the Social Security Home No. 2
proposed.zh: 社会保障局 / 社保二号养老院
proposed.ja: 社会保障局／社会保障局第二ホーム

terms.gloss: People's Commissariat for Foreign Trade
terms.why_hard: Standard Soviet acronym; keep one consistent expansion scheme for all Нарком- bodies

proposed.en: the People's Commissariat for Foreign Trade

terms.gloss: People's Commissariat of Education, which sent ten chairs to the Moscow furniture museum
terms.why_hard: Plot-critical: the ten chairs went via a Narkompros circular; must be the same name later in Moscow chapters

terms.gloss: Glavchai, the Central Tea Administration (state tea trust)
terms.why_hard: Reader will not know it is a tea trust; the comedy is a dining set going to the tea bureau

terms.gloss: Municipal housing department and its head (who allocated rooms and furniture)
terms.why_hard: 'Зав-' and 'т.' are abbreviations for 'head of' and 'comrade'; expand them

proposed.en: the Housing Department / head of the Housing Department
proposed.zh: 住房处 / 住房处主任

terms.gloss: Water-transport (river and sea) workers' club
terms.why_hard: 'Водник' is a trade-union category, not 'water man' or 'sailor'

terms.gloss: The Moscow Museum of Furniture Craft, where ten of the chairs went
terms.why_hard: Plot-critical destination that recurs; fix one name now

terms.gloss: Disabled veteran of the First World War, in official Soviet phrasing ('the imperialist war')
terms.why_hard: Do not normalize to 'World War I'; the Soviet label is part of the bureaucratic parody

proposed.en: a disabled veteran of the Imperialist War
proposed.zh: 帝国主义战争残废军人
proposed.ja: 帝国主義戦争の傷痍軍人

terms.gloss: Made by Gambs, a famous Petersburg furniture-maker; the twelve chairs are 'Gambs chairs' throughout the book
terms.why_hard: The book's most repeated epithet; must be one form (Gambs) in every chapter

terms.gloss: A grand piano by J. Becker, the leading Petersburg piano firm
terms.why_hard: 'Рояль' is a grand, not an upright; brand name should be kept as Becker

proposed.ja: ベッカー製グランドピアノ

terms.gloss: Aubusson (French), Tekke (Turkmen) and Khorasan (Persian) carpets
terms.why_hard: Standard art-trade names exist in each language; do not transliterate from Russian

proposed.zh: 奥比松、特克、呼罗珊地毯
proposed.ja: オービュッソン、テッケ、ホラーサーン絨毯

terms.gloss: Two tapestries, 'The Shepherdess' and 'The Shepherd', from the Vorobyaninov house
terms.why_hard: Titles recur (the Shepherdess is later retrieved); keep both as fixed quoted titles

proposed.ja: タペストリー「牧羊女」／「牧人」

terms.gloss: Bender quoting Pushkin's 'Exegi monumentum' ('I have raised a monument not made by hands')
terms.why_hard: A literal 'handmade monument' loses the quotation; use the recognizable Pushkin wording in each language

proposed.en: a monument not made by hands (Pushkin)
proposed.zh: 非人手所建的纪念碑（普希金）
proposed.ja: 人の手によらぬ記念碑（プーシキン）

terms.gloss: Bender's catchphrase: he misuses 'congenial' to mean 'brilliant, genius-level'
terms.why_hard: It is a deliberate malapropism and recurs; rendering must be the same odd word every time

terms.gloss: Requisition/distribution warrants (green counterfoils) recording who got each piece of furniture
terms.why_hard: Not military 'orders' or medals; the word recurs in the plot as the paper trail

terms.gloss: Pious formula for the dead, 'may he rest in the Kingdom of Heaven'
terms.why_hard: Marks the old archivist's pre-revolutionary piety; use a churchy idiom, not a neutral 'the late'

conventions: Soviet acronyms: expand into the reader's language on every occurrence (City Military Commissariat, Housing Department); keep a transliteration plus one expansion only where the acronym itself is the joke (Starprodkomgub) or is plot-critical and famous (Narkompros).

Korobeinikov's old-regime deference (Вот-с, Пожа-алуйста) and provincial forms (куды, посейчас) are rendered as polite-archaic register: en 'Here you are, sir'; zh 老派客套的"您"; ja ございます-style keigo, never dialect spelling.
Dialogue: Russian em-dash speech becomes en double quotes, zh curly double quotes, ja 「」; the narrator's asides stay in the same dry register with no added exclamation.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the provincial priest who chases the chairs on his own account
terms.why_hard: Spelling of the name must be fixed once (Fyodor vs Feodor vs Fedor); 'отец' is a clerical title, not 'father' in the family sense

terms.gloss: the customary title for an Orthodox priest's wife (here Father Fyodor's wife)
terms.why_hard: Literal 'mother'/'little mother' is wrong; it is the priest's wife, and the word recurs whenever she appears

terms.gloss: Prusis, a NEP-era private stall-keeper (owner of a market booth) in Father Fyodor's town
terms.why_hard: 'палаточник' is a small private trader with a market stall, not a tent-maker or camper; name transliteration must be fixed

terms.gloss: financial agent: the local tax inspector of the NEP period who assessed and collected taxes from private traders
terms.why_hard: Not a 'financial agent' or broker; the joke is that the trader is buying beer for the man who taxes him

terms.gloss: a slow passenger train that also carried mail (a class of train, below express)
terms.why_hard: Not a train carrying only mail; it is the cheap slow passenger service

terms.gloss: a train with no reserved seats, boarded in a free-for-all
terms.why_hard: Explains the 'scandalous' boarding scene; 'unreserved' must be kept, and the same term recurs whenever the heroes travel cheap

proposed.en: a train with no reserved seats

terms.gloss: laymen, non-clergy; the priest in mufti feels his striped trousers exposed 'to the eyes of all the laity'
terms.why_hard: The comedy is a priest thinking in church categories on a railway platform; flattening to 'everyone' loses it

terms.gloss: the railway right-of-way, the strip of land legally alienated to the railway; the narrator mocks the citizen who 'amateurishly' calls it a station
terms.why_hard: Must be a dry legal-technical term in the target language, since the joke is bureaucratic jargon versus the plain word 'station'

terms.gloss: 'citizen', the neutral Soviet form of reference and address for anyone (as opposed to 'comrade')
terms.why_hard: Rendering as 'man', 'person' or 'gentleman' loses the period flavour; must be one fixed word book-wide

terms.gloss: Yermak Timofeyevich, the bearded Cossack conqueror of Siberia; the porters are burly bearded men in white aprons likened to him
terms.why_hard: A pluralised proper name used as an epithet; the reader needs the image (bearded giants), not just a transliterated name

proposed.en: porters built like Yermak the Cossack
proposed.zh: 叶尔马克式的大胡子壮汉搬运工
proposed.ja: コサックの豪傑エルマークさながらの赤帽たち

terms.gloss: the nickel-plated numbered badges worn on the chest by licensed station porters
terms.why_hard: 'бляха' is a badge/plate, not a buckle; 'on the heart' is the narrator's mock-solemn placement

terms.gloss: consignee, the bureaucratic term for a person receiving freight
terms.why_hard: Part of the mock-official taxonomy (passenger / consignee / ticketless bum); needs the same dry register

terms.gloss: a ticketless drunken layabout haunting stations
terms.why_hard: 'забулдыга' is colloquial, a boozy bum; too formal or too vulgar breaks the comic list

terms.gloss: the train conductor crews and the ticket inspectors at platform gates
terms.why_hard: Two distinct railway roles; also distinct from 'проводник' (car attendant) whom passengers plead with

proposed.zh: 列车员班组和站台查票员
proposed.ja: 車掌班とホームの検札係

terms.gloss: the attendant of a railway carriage (Russian 'provodnik'), who admits passengers and manages the car
terms.why_hard: Not a 'guide' or 'conductor'; should be kept distinct from кондуктор throughout the book

terms.gloss: a short oral joke with a punchline, the staple of Russian train conversation
terms.why_hard: The false friend 'anecdote' is wrong; these are jokes

terms.term: Умирает старый еврей... Кто же в лавке остался?!
terms.gloss: a classic Odessa-style Jewish joke: the dying shopkeeper's last worry is who is minding the shop
terms.why_hard: The Jewish jokes are period Odessa humour told by the passengers, not the narrator; render plainly, neither softening 'a Jew' nor adding slurs; keep the punchline last

proposed.en: An old Jew is dying... 'Then who's minding the shop?!'
proposed.zh: 一个犹太老头快死了……“那铺子里还剩谁看着？！”
proposed.ja: 年老いたユダヤ人が死にかけている……「じゃあ店には誰が残ってるんだ？！」

terms.gloss: Yiddish-inflected family names in the deathbed joke (Monya, Aunt Brana, Isak)
terms.why_hard: Should be transliterated consistently and keep their Yiddish colouring (Isak, not Isaac)

proposed.zh: 莫尼亚、布拉娜阿姨、伊萨克
proposed.ja: モーニャ、ブラーナおばさん、イサーク

terms.gloss: Jack, a dog's name, the punchline of the second joke ('Is that you, Jack?' - the dog licks his hand)
terms.why_hard: The English dog-name must stay recognisable as a pet's name so the punchline lands

terms.gloss: railway semaphore signals imagined as prim figures in glowing green spectacles looking over the train
terms.why_hard: The personification (spectacles, 'fastidiously', 'looking over the top of the train') is the narrator's signature; keep the semaphore concrete and the image intact

proposed.en: slender semaphores in glowing green spectacles
proposed.zh: 戴着发亮绿眼镜的细长臂板信号机
proposed.ja: 光る緑の眼鏡をかけた細身の腕木信号機

terms.gloss: the station buffet, a snack bar serving beer and food
terms.why_hard: Not a sideboard or a buffet-style meal

terms.gloss: chapter title, 'The Muse of Distant Wanderings', echoing Gumilyov's 1910 poem cycle 'Discovery of America'
terms.why_hard: A Silver Age poetic phrase used mock-solemnly for a slow train; the rendering should sound lofty, and the allusion may need a one-line note

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash speech becomes double quotation marks in English, “ ” in Chinese, 「 」 in Japanese; jokes quoted inside dialogue use single quotes / ‘ ’ / 『 』
Chapter headings: 'Глава IV' → 'Chapter Four' / '第四章' / '第四章', with the title on the same line after a period or full-width colon
'гражданин' is always 'citizen' / 公民 / 市民, never 'comrade', 'man' or 'gentleman'; Japanese names of Russian characters use ・ between given name and surname and take no honorific in narration

terms.gloss: The great schemer, protagonist con man; narrator calls him Остап, Бендер, and by mock-epithets by turns
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Ostap Bender, not Ostap Bender/Benders) and zh/ja phonetic renderings must not drift between pages

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former Stargorod housing-office archivist who keeps the furniture requisition records; neighbours call him Варфоломеич
terms.why_hard: Three forms (surname, full name, patronymic-only nickname) must map to three consistent renderings; the patronymic alone signals familiar contempt

proposed.zh: 瓦尔福洛梅·科罗贝尼科夫／瓦尔福洛梅伊奇
proposed.ja: ヴァルフォロメイ・コロベイニコフ／ヴァルフォロメイチ

terms.gloss: Archivist; Korobeinikov's old job title, used by the narrator as his standing epithet
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as generic 'clerk' or 'record-keeper' loses the dusty pre-revolutionary officialese the narrator is mocking

terms.gloss: Post-revolutionary requisition orders assigning confiscated furniture to new owners or institutions; the stubs record where each piece went
terms.why_hard: 'Orders' in English reads as commands; the reader must understand these are paper allocation warrants that trace the chairs

terms.gloss: Counterfoil stubs of the requisition orders, bearing recipients' addresses and signatures
terms.why_hard: Literal 'spines' or 'roots' is wrong; it is the stub of a tear-off form

terms.gloss: Made by Gambs, the celebrated Petersburg furniture firm of Heinrich Gambs; the twelve chairs are Gambs chairs and this recurs through the book
terms.why_hard: Must be a proper name recognizable as a brand each time, not 'Hambs' or a descriptive paraphrase

terms.gloss: General Popov's wife or widow, former owner of a confiscated furniture set
terms.why_hard: генеральша is a wife by rank, not a female general; zh/ja must not produce a woman general

terms.gloss: 'Fighter for the idea', Soviet phrase for a principled revolutionary, used by Ostap as a mocking address to a profiteer
terms.why_hard: Translate the cliche as a cliche so the sarcasm lands; a neutral 'idealist' kills it

terms.gloss: Card-table/Odessa slang: 'go ahead, deal, cover it'; Ostap's brisk go-ahead
terms.why_hard: Not the dictionary 'cut cloth'; needs a punchy colloquial one-worder consistent wherever Ostap uses it

terms.gloss: 'Chief concessionaire', narrator's mock-business epithet for Ostap, from the 'concession' he has formed with Vorobyaninov to hunt the chairs
terms.why_hard: The NEP joke of a foreign-style concession must be kept as a fixed epithet across the book, not paraphrased as 'the leader'

proposed.ja: コンセッションの総帥

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary rank: head of a governor's or ministry chancery; Ostap flatters the archivist with an obsolete grand title
terms.why_hard: Rendering as 'office manager' loses the antique pomp; keep it audibly tsarist

terms.gloss: Familiar, oily endearment ('my dove, dear fellow'), Odessa flavour, in Ostap's mouth patronizing
terms.why_hard: Must sound affectionate and insolent at once; 'darling' is too warm, 'friend' too flat

terms.gloss: Ostap's recurring oath on the honour of his late father (whose identity he keeps changing, e.g. 'son of a Turkish subject')
terms.why_hard: Recurs across the book; render батюшка with the same word each time so the running gag about the father is traceable

proposed.en: I swear on the honour of my late papa
proposed.ja: 亡き父の名誉にかけて誓う

terms.gloss: Current (checking) bank account; Ostap invokes one he plainly does not have
terms.why_hard: Anachronistic-sounding banking term; keep it deadpan and modern-sounding, not 'running account'

terms.gloss: 'I'm telling you in plain Russian'; impatient insistence that one has been perfectly clear
terms.why_hard: Do not literalize 'in the Russian language' for a zh/ja reader; use the target idiom for 'in plain words'

proposed.en: I'm telling you in plain Russian
proposed.ja: はっきり言っているだろう

terms.gloss: 'Write letters!' -- flippant farewell meaning 'you'll never see me again'; became a Russian catchphrase from this novel
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering is opaque; needs a dismissive brush-off that can recur verbatim

terms.gloss: 'The ice has broken, gentlemen of the jury!' -- Ostap's signature exclamation when the scheme starts moving; the most famous line of the book
terms.why_hard: Must be fixed verbatim book-wide; the mock-courtroom address to jurors is part of the joke and must not be dropped

proposed.en: The ice is breaking, gentlemen of the jury!
proposed.zh: 冰层开动了，陪审员先生们！
proposed.ja: 氷が動き出したぞ、陪審員諸君！

terms.gloss: Krasny Treugolnik ('Red Triangle'), the Petersburg/Leningrad rubber-goods factory whose galoshes carried a red triangle trademark
terms.why_hard: The ashtray shaped like a galosh with the 'Triangle' brand is a period product joke; a bare 'Triangle' needs the galosh context kept

proposed.ja: 「トレウゴーリニク」（三角印ゴム工場）

terms.gloss: Poor outlying quarter of Stargorod where Korobeinikov lives and lends at usurious rates
terms.why_hard: A fictional toponym; transliterate once and never translate it as 'Goose Place'

terms.gloss: 'Cannibal interest rates', i.e. usurious
terms.why_hard: Keep the grotesque image rather than flattening to 'exorbitant'

terms.gloss: The 'Shepherdess' tapestry, part of the walnut drawing-room set lost with the requisition orders; recurs later in the book
terms.why_hard: Title of a work of art in quotes; keep the same title form each time it reappears

proposed.ja: ゴブラン織「牧羊の乙女」

terms.gloss: Mechanical twist doorbell with the enamel sign 'please turn' (i.e. crank)
terms.why_hard: A pre-electric bell; the quoted sign is a period object, do not turn it into a push-button

proposed.ja: 「お回しください」と書かれた呼び鈴

conventions: Dialogue: replace Russian em-dash lines with quotation marks in en (double), zh (“ ”), ja (「 」); keep one speech per paragraph as in the source.
Ostap's ты/вы shifts (e.g. polite вы to the archivist, then 'Тише, дурак' with ты) are marked in ja by dropping to plain form and in zh by switching 您→你; en uses tone and address words instead.
Narrator's mock-epithets for Ostap (великий комбинатор, главный концессионер, технический директор) are fixed strings book-wide and are never replaced by his name.
