terms.gloss: Treukhov, the modest, obsessive Stargorod engineer who has dreamed for years of building the town tramway; hero of chapter XIII.
terms.why_hard: Name recurs across the chapter and must be transliterated identically; the -ух- must not become -uch-/-ukh- inconsistently.

terms.gloss: Gavrilin, head of the Stargorod communal services (Starkomkhoz), Treukhov's blunt, plain-spoken boss and patron.
terms.why_hard: Speaks to Treukhov as ты with worker's familiarity ('начинай', 'То-то'); his register must stay consistent wherever he appears.

terms.gloss: Stargorod ('Old Town'), the fictional provincial capital where the first half of the novel is set; its inhabitants.
terms.why_hard: A fictional name that must not be translated ('Oldtown') in one place and transliterated in another; the demonym needs a fixed form too.

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔哥罗德 / 斯塔尔哥罗德人
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド / スタルゴロドの人々

terms.gloss: The local Party daily, 'Stargorod Truth', modelled on the provincial Pravdas of the 1920s.
terms.why_hard: Pravda should be kept recognisable as the Soviet newspaper name rather than translated to a bland 'Truth'; fix one form for all occurrences.

terms.gloss: The tramway power station (electric generating plant) that Treukhov is building, together with the depot.
terms.why_hard: Not a tram stop: 'station' here means powerhouse, and the whole chapter's ceremony is the opening of the power station.

terms.gloss: Food Trust, a NEP-era state trust grouping the provincial food-processing enterprises; asked to buy shares in the tram company.
terms.why_hard: A portmanteau acronym typical of the era; must be expanded so the reader sees a state enterprise, not a brand, and kept identical each time.

terms.gloss: Maslotsentr, the All-Russian central union of dairy (butter) co-operatives.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'Butter Centre' sounds like a shop; it is a co-operative headquarters, one of the era's many -центр organisations.

proposed.ja: 乳製品協同組合センター

terms.gloss: The rope-works: workers/management of the Stargorod rope factory, whose freight must be hauled to the railway station.
terms.why_hard: Colloquial metonymy (people for factory); a translator may miss that Gavrilin means the factory as a prospective shareholder.

terms.gloss: People's Commissariat of Railways (Narodny komissariat putey soobshcheniya), the central transport ministry.
terms.why_hard: Opaque acronym; render as the ministry it is, not as letters, and keep one rendering with the other Narkomats in the book.

terms.gloss: Provincial Executive Committee, the government of a guberniya (province) under the Soviets; its presidium decides the tram question.
terms.why_hard: Contracted Soviet compound; 'gubernia' should be rendered consistently as 'province' throughout, and 'presidium' kept as a term.

terms.gloss: The State Bank of the USSR and the Communal (municipal services) Bank, both lenders to local infrastructure.
terms.why_hard: Kombank is not a 'commercial bank' but the Kommunalny (municipal) bank; the pair should read as two distinct state lenders.

proposed.en: the State Bank and the Municipal Bank
proposed.ja: 国立銀行と地方公営銀行

terms.gloss: Provincial Control Commission of the Party, the disciplinary body to which Gavrilin is summoned 'for pressure' on shareholders.
terms.why_hard: A Party, not a state, body; the joke is that strong-arming for a good cause earns a Party disciplinary hearing.

terms.gloss: A joint-stock company, the NEP-era legal form used to pool state and co-operative capital for the tramway.
terms.why_hard: Keep the capitalist term deliberately: the humour is that a Soviet tram is financed by 'shareholders' haggling over 15% vs 10%.

terms.gloss: Horse-drawn haulage, the cartage system the tram is meant to replace.
terms.why_hard: Mock-official term used in a domestic scene (Treukhov lectures his wife while washing laundry); the stiffness must be kept.

terms.gloss: 'This isn't like buying a donkey' — Gavrilin's gruff catchphrase; ешак is a dialectal form of ишак (donkey).
terms.why_hard: The nonstandard 'ешак' marks Gavrilin as uneducated; the phrase recurs in his speech and should be word-for-word identical each time.

proposed.en: This isn't like buying a donkey, you know.
proposed.zh: 这可不是买头驴那么简单。
proposed.ja: ロバを買うのとは話が違うんだぞ。

terms.gloss: Creosote-impregnated railway sleepers and the plant that treats them.
terms.why_hard: US 'ties' vs UK 'sleepers' must be chosen once; 'impregnated' is the industry term, not 'soaked'.

proposed.zh: 防腐轨枕 / 轨枕防腐厂
proposed.ja: 防腐処理済み枕木 / 枕木防腐工場

terms.term: фасонное железо; раковины в чугунных частях
terms.gloss: Rolled section iron (structural shapes), and blowholes (casting cavities) in the cast-iron parts.
terms.why_hard: 'Раковины' is not 'shells' or 'sinks' here but foundry cavities; the list of defects should sound like an engineer's report.

proposed.en: section iron; blowholes in the castings
proposed.ja: 形鋼；鋳鉄部品に巣（鋳巣）

terms.gloss: Gavrilin's old Fiat car described as 'having a cold' — wheezing and coughing.
terms.why_hard: The personification is the joke; a flat 'rattling old Fiat' loses it, and the car recurs in the chapter.

proposed.en: an old Fiat with a head cold
proposed.zh: 一辆患了感冒的旧菲亚特
proposed.ja: 風邪をひいた古いフィアット

terms.gloss: A feuilletonist: writer of the satirical/topical column in a newspaper, a prestigious Soviet journalistic genre (Ilf and Petrov's own trade).
terms.why_hard: No exact English equivalent; 'columnist' is close but 'satirical columnist' carries the genre. Fix one term for the whole book.

proposed.zh: 小品文作家（专栏讽刺作家）

terms.gloss: 'Prince of Denmark' (Hamlet), the old pen-name of the town's feuilletonist, now writing as Makhovik.
terms.why_hard: The allusion to Hamlet must stay visible; the contrast between a decadent literary pseudonym and a new industrial one is the point.

terms.gloss: 'Flywheel', the columnist's new, production-minded pseudonym under which he writes upbeat construction sketches.
terms.why_hard: Must be translated (the meaning is the joke), then used as a name; keep it in quotation marks or capitals as a proper noun.

terms.gloss: A 'sketch of everyday life', the Soviet reportage genre Makhovik writes three times a week about the construction.
terms.why_hard: 'Everyday sketch' is opaque; 'human-interest feature' conveys the genre to a modern reader.

terms.gloss: Headline: 'Tighten the screws on the wreckers of education' — вредители ('wreckers') is the Soviet label for saboteurs.
terms.why_hard: 'Wreckers' is the established English term for вредители and should be used here and wherever the word recurs.

proposed.en: Tighten the Screws on the Wreckers of Education
proposed.zh: 《拧紧教育界破坏分子的螺丝》
proposed.ja: 「教育界の破壊者を締め上げよ」

terms.gloss: Headline: 'Time to end the sea of paper', i.e. bureaucratic red tape.
terms.why_hard: Standard 1920s press cliche; render as a plausible headline, not a literal image, and keep 'paper' for the бумажный motif elsewhere.

proposed.en: Time to Drain the Sea of Paperwork

terms.term: «На берегу пустынных волн стоял он, дум великих полн»
terms.gloss: Opening lines of Pushkin's 'The Bronze Horseman' (Peter the Great planning Petersburg), pompously applied by Makhovik to Treukhov.
terms.why_hard: Every Russian reader recognises it; the translation must be verse-like and a short note should name Pushkin, or the parody vanishes.

proposed.en: 'Upon the shore of desolate waves he stood, and mighty thoughts he brooded.' (Pushkin, The Bronze Horseman)
proposed.zh: “荒凉的波涛岸边，他伫立着，满怀宏图伟略。”（普希金《青铜骑士》）
proposed.ja: 「寂しき波の岸辺に彼は立ちて、大いなる思いに満ちていた」（プーシキン『青銅の騎士』）

terms.gloss: The engineer's service cap with a crossed-hammers badge, the insignia of railway and technical personnel.
terms.why_hard: 'Cap with little hammers' baffles the reader; it marks Treukhov as a trained engineer and recurs as his identifying detail.

proposed.en: a shabby engineer's cap with the crossed-hammers badge
proposed.zh: 一顶带交叉锤徽的旧工程师帽
proposed.ja: ハンマーの徽章のついたよれよれの技師帽

terms.gloss: 'Brother writers', an ironic collective for journalists, echoing Pushkin's 'братья-разбойники' and the trade-guild phrase.
terms.why_hard: Ironic register: Treukhov's disgust with 'the writing fraternity'; a neutral 'writers' loses the sneer.

conventions: Soviet acronyms and portmanteau institutions (Пищетрест, НКПС, губисполком, ГубКК, Госбанк) are expanded into a descriptive rendering in all three languages rather than kept as letters; the Russian abbreviation appears only in the source column.

Dialogue dashes are converted to the target language's quotation conventions: English double quotes, Chinese “ ”, Japanese 「 」; the narrator's dry interjections stay in the same sentence as in the Russian.

Gavrilin addresses Treukhov as ты in a worker's plain register: render with contractions and blunt imperatives in English, plain 你 in Chinese, and plain-form (だ/ぞ) speech without honorifics in Japanese; Treukhov's replies use formal register.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The widow Gritsatsuyeva, Stargorod grocer whom Bender later marries for her chair; her name recurs through the book.
terms.why_hard: The surname must be transliterated identically everywhere; zh/ja renderings of a long Ukrainian-flavoured surname drift easily between pages.

proposed.ja: 未亡人グリツァツーエワ

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the ex-marshal of the nobility; the narrator names him by name and patronymic throughout.
terms.why_hard: Dropping the patronymic or switching between Vorobyaninov/Ippolit Matveyevich page by page loses the mock-respectful tone.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, fortune-teller, once Vorobyaninov's mistress; three forms of her name occur on one page.
terms.why_hard: The three forms (name-patronymic, madame + surname, name + surname) must map to one recognisable person in each language; 'madame' is ironic here.

proposed.en: Elena Stanislavovna / Madame Bour / Elena Bour
proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜 / 鲍乌尔太太 / 叶莲娜·鲍乌尔
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ / マダム・ボウル / エレーナ・ボウル

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the Stargorod mechanic, busybody and future 'conspirator'; recurring character.
terms.why_hard: Consistent transliteration; the narrator uses the full name-patronymic as a comic formality that should be kept.

proposed.zh: 维克多·米哈伊洛维奇·波列索夫
proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

terms.gloss: Polesov's standing epithet: a metal-fitter who considers himself an intellectual (and belongs to no workshop, mends nothing to the end).
terms.why_hard: 'Locksmith' is wrong (слесарь = fitter/mechanic); the hyphenated epithet must be one fixed phrase wherever it recurs.

terms.gloss: Stargorod ('Old Town'), the fictional provincial town where the first part of the novel is set.
terms.why_hard: Must not be translated ('Oldtown') or confused with real Starodub/Stary Oskol; fixed transliteration in zh/ja.

terms.gloss: The Last Judgment; here the widow's life line runs so far she would 'live to see the Last Judgment'.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'terrible court' loses the fixed Christian term; zh/ja must use the standard theological phrase.

terms.gloss: Palmistry term: the Mount of Venus (the ball of the thumb), read as an index of love and sensuality.
terms.why_hard: Palmistry has fixed vocabulary in every target language; a made-up rendering breaks the joke of the fortune-teller's pseudo-science.

terms.gloss: The hills of Manchuria, evoking the Russo-Japanese War and the waltz 'On the Hills of Manchuria' (1906) every 1928 reader knew.
terms.why_hard: 'Sopka' is a specific Far-Eastern word for a hill; the waltz echo is lost if rendered as generic 'mountains'.

terms.gloss: Horse-dealers, proverbially glib swindlers; listed with graphologists and palmists as users of the same jargon.
terms.why_hard: Needs the sly connotation of the horse-trader as con man, not a neutral 'horse merchant'.

terms.gloss: Petty-bourgeois provincial diminutive of 'madame', the widow's ingratiating address to the fortune-teller.
terms.why_hard: The comic diminutive marks the widow's social register; a flat 'madam' is too formal, 'dear' too warm.

terms.gloss: Cartomancy figures: the king of clubs (a dark-haired man, i.e. Vorobyaninov) and the queen of diamonds (a rival woman).
terms.why_hard: Card names must follow the standard suit terms of each language and stay identical when the widow later recalls them.

proposed.en: the king of clubs / the queen of diamonds
proposed.zh: 梅花国王 / 方块王后
proposed.ja: クラブのキング / ダイヤのクイーン

terms.gloss: Fortune-tellers' jargon (from French mariage): a 'marrying' king, a suitor fated to wed the querent.
terms.why_hard: The widow is asking whether the man will marry her; a literal 'marital king' is opaque, but the term must stay a cartomancy word.

terms.gloss: A 'Graetz' kerosene stove, a German brand common in Russian kitchens before and after the Revolution.
terms.why_hard: Brand name should be transliterated as a brand, not translated or dropped; the kerosene stove itself is a period object.

proposed.ja: グレーツ製の石油コンロ

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary court clerk (secretary of the district court), a minor official who wrote verse to Madame Bour.
terms.why_hard: Not a 'court secretary' in the modern office sense; the mild pomposity of the old rank is part of the joke.

terms.gloss: A line of bad provincial album verse about the young Elena Bour, quoted as a recurring epithet for her.
terms.why_hard: It must read as doggerel and be reproduced verbatim each time it recurs; its contrast with her present state is the point.

proposed.en: 'so airy, so inviting to be kissed'
proposed.zh: “召人亲吻的她，浑身轻盈如空气”
proposed.ja: 「口づけを誘う、まるで空気のような彼女」

terms.gloss: Polesov's face compared to an operatic devil (Mephistopheles) smeared with soot before going on stage.
terms.why_hard: A vague 'devil' loses the theatrical image; the opera reference and the soot-makeup should survive in all three languages.

terms.gloss: Three-eighths-inch threading dies; imperial thread sizes were still standard in Soviet workshops.
terms.why_hard: Must be the tool (die), not 'plates'; the inch fraction should be kept, not metricised, since the joke depends on the specificity.

terms.gloss: The Stargorod tram, the town's long-promised municipal project that Polesov derides; a running motif of the Stargorod chapters.
terms.why_hard: Choose one word (tram vs streetcar) for the whole book; zh/ja have fixed terms.

terms.term: хореографические курсы имени Леонардо да Винчи
terms.gloss: Parody of the Soviet mania for naming institutions after unrelated great men: dance courses 'named after Leonardo da Vinci'.
terms.why_hard: The 'имени X' formula must be rendered consistently for every named institution in the book; the absurdity is in the mismatch.

proposed.en: the Leonardo da Vinci Choreography Courses
proposed.zh: 列奥纳多·达·芬奇舞蹈进修班
proposed.ja: レオナルド・ダ・ヴィンチ記念舞踊講習会

terms.gloss: Joke that a dance student thinks curd cheese is 'mined' from vareniki (Ukrainian dumplings stuffed with curd).
terms.why_hard: Both foods need a rendering the reader knows; 'cottage cheese from dumplings' works only if the dumpling is identified as curd-filled.

proposed.en: curd cheese is extracted from vareniki dumplings
proposed.zh: 酸奶渣是从瓦列尼基饺子里挖出来的
proposed.ja: カッテージチーズはワレーニキ（餃子）から採れる

terms.gloss: A comic Soviet acronym for a Stargorod trading co-operative ('Stargorod Co-op'); the widow finds such names 'dreadful'.
terms.why_hard: Must remain an ugly acronym in each language, with a one-word expansion at first use; other pages will carry more such names.

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈科（斯塔尔戈罗德合作社）
proposed.ja: スタルギコ（スタルゴロド協同組合）

terms.gloss: The General Electric Company (the pre-revolutionary Russian branch of AEG/GE) whose four surviving tram motors are the only good ones.
terms.why_hard: Translate as the actual company name, not word for word; whether AEG or American GE is meant affects the rendering.

proposed.ja: ゼネラル・エレクトリック社

terms.gloss: 'Kharkov work': made in Kharkov, then capital of Soviet Ukraine, i.e. new Soviet manufacture, implied to be shoddy.
terms.why_hard: Spelling (Kharkov/Kharkiv) must be fixed for the whole book; the sneer at Soviet-made goods is the point.

terms.gloss: Soviet trust acronym (State Non-Ferrous Metals Industry), used by Polesov as a byword for junk workmanship.
terms.why_hard: Should stay an acronym with a short in-text expansion; translating it as plain 'state metal' loses the bureaucratic ugliness.

proposed.en: Gospromtsvetmet (the State Non-Ferrous Metals Trust) through and through
proposed.zh: 地地道道的“国营有色金属”货
proposed.ja: まるごと国営非鉄金属工業（ゴスプロムツヴェトメト）製

terms.gloss: Verst, the old Russian mile (about 1.07 km), still used colloquially in 1928.
terms.why_hard: Keep as 'verst' (with zh/ja standard renderings) rather than converting to kilometres, and use the same choice book-wide.

terms.gloss: Polesov's habitual exclamation ('darkness'), meaning 'hopeless, a disaster'.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'Darkness!' is meaningless; it needs one punchy fixed rendering since it is his catchphrase.

terms.gloss: 'What we have lived to see', the grumbling formula of the ex-bourgeois about Soviet shortages.
terms.why_hard: Should be a natural idiom of complaint, matched consistently when other characters use it.

proposed.zh: 咱们都活到什么份儿上了
proposed.ja: なんという時代になったものだ

conventions: Personal names: en transliteration without diacritics (Gritsatsuyeva, Vorobyaninov), zh standard Xinhua-style syllables with interpunct, ja katakana with nakaguro; keep name + patronymic wherever the narrator uses it, never substitute the surname.
Dialogue: replace the Russian dash-dialogue with double quotation marks in en, “” in zh and 「」 in ja; narrator's asides stay in the same sentence, set off by commas or dashes, not parentheses.
Soviet acronyms (Старгико, госпромцветмет and the like): transliterate as a proper noun and add a two-to-four-word expansion in brackets at first occurrence only, never a footnote.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ostap's invented monarchist underground; a pun on Isaiah's 'swords into ploughshares' (орало = ploughshare) that also sounds like орать (to bawl)
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as a plain 'Sword and Plough Union' loses the biblical echo; must be fixed once since it names chapter XIV and recurs as a running joke

proposed.en: The Union of the Sword and Ploughshare

terms.term: гигант мысли, отец русской демократии и особа, приближенная к императору
terms.gloss: Ostap's mock title for Vorobyaninov, repeated verbatim through the chapter and later; became a Russian catchphrase
terms.why_hard: It is repeated as a formula (here twice, in full and shortened); every language needs one fixed, pompous, quotable wording reused each time

proposed.en: a giant of thought, father of Russian democracy and a person close to the Emperor
proposed.zh: 思想的巨人、俄国民主之父、皇帝身边的红人
proposed.ja: 思想の巨人、ロシア民主主義の父にして皇帝の側近

terms.gloss: The 'great schemer', con man protagonist; also called Остап, Бендер
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed across the book; zh/ja have established forms from published translations

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, the second concessionaire; narrator alternates between name+patronymic and surname
terms.why_hard: Keep both forms distinct and consistent (Ippolit Matveyevich vs Vorobyaninov); do not collapse to one, the alternation carries tone

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 / 沃罗比扬尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ / ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Stargorod's hysterical 'genius locksmith', busybody mechanic obsessed with gates and trams
terms.why_hard: Appears as Полесов and as Виктор Михайлович in the same page; the two must map to one recognizable person

proposed.zh: 维克多·米哈伊洛维奇·波列索夫
proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

terms.gloss: Fortune-teller (гадалка), Vorobyaninov's old flame, hostess of the meeting; her parrot is a recurring prop
terms.why_hard: Polish-sounding patronymic; also referred to simply as 'гадалка', which should stay 'the fortune-teller' rather than 'sorceress'

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: Former member of the pre-revolutionary city duma, now a Soviet office worker
terms.why_hard: Surname transliteration (Charushnikov) and the joke about his 'canonization' must be kept together

proposed.zh: 马克西姆·彼得罗维奇·恰鲁什尼科夫
proposed.ja: マクシム・ペトローヴィチ・チャルシニコフ

terms.gloss: Owner of the 'Bystroupak' firm, the richest man among the conspirators
terms.why_hard: Soft sign in the middle: Dyadyev, not Dyadev; keep one spelling

terms.gloss: Chairman of the bagel-makers' artel, chronically frightened; recurring victim of Ostap later in the book
terms.why_hard: Recurs many chapters later (the 'Union' extortions); spelling must match

terms.gloss: Two nameless 'young men' (Nikesha, Vladya): affectionate diminutives of Nikifor/Vladimir
terms.why_hard: The point is that they have pet-names but 'no surnames'; keep the diminutives, do not expand to full names

proposed.ja: ニケーシャとヴラージャ

terms.gloss: Madame Gritsatsuyeva, the 'passionate woman, a poet's dream', whom Ostap marries next day for a chair
terms.why_hard: The 'wedding' mentioned here refers to her; name must match its later chapters

proposed.ja: 未亡人グリツァツーエワ

terms.gloss: Narrator's standing epithet for Ostap and Vorobyaninov, from Ostap's joke that their treasure hunt is a 'concession' (NEP-era foreign concessions)
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed word book-wide; 'partners' loses the NEP joke

proposed.ja: コンセッション屋たち

terms.gloss: Ostap's ironic address to Vorobyaninov as 'boss/patron'
terms.why_hard: Not 'cartridge'; keep the same mock-deferential form each time Ostap uses it

terms.gloss: Polesov's meaningless bureaucratic phrase 'given the presence of an absence'; became proverbial for empty officialese
terms.why_hard: Must sound like real jargon gone wrong, not a translation error; keep stable since it typifies Polesov

proposed.en: In the presence of an absence…
proposed.ja: 不在の存在に鑑みまして……

terms.gloss: Elected member of a pre-1917 municipal duma (city council)
terms.why_hard: гласный here is a noun (councillor), not 'vowel' or 'public'

proposed.en: former member of the city duma

terms.gloss: Church formula 'numbered among the saints' applied to becoming a Soviet employee (совработник = советский работник)
terms.why_hard: Two layers: the ecclesiastical verb and the Soviet acronym; a flat 'became a Soviet employee' kills the joke

proposed.en: miraculously canonized among the ranks of Soviet employees
proposed.zh: 奇迹般地被册封为苏维埃职员
proposed.ja: 奇跡的に「ソヴィエト勤務員」の列聖に加えられた

terms.gloss: NEP-era private firm, a parody of Soviet portmanteau names ('Quick-Pack')
terms.why_hard: Should read as a name yet let the reader catch the 'quick packing' parody; keep the same form in narration and dialogue

terms.gloss: Kislyarsky's cooperative: an Odessa bagel artel named 'Moscow Baranki' (the joke is the two rival ring-bread names, бублик vs баранка)
terms.why_hard: артель is a cooperative, not a factory; бублик and баранка are both ring-shaped breads and should not both become 'bagel'

proposed.zh: “莫斯科小面包圈”敖德萨大面包圈手工业合作社
proposed.ja: オデッサ・ブーブリク組合「モスクワ・バランカ」

terms.gloss: Building yardman/caretaker, in the 1920s also an informal police informant
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' misses that a дворник was a street-level authority figure, which is why Polesov resents him

terms.gloss: Boor, lout, from the biblical Ham; pre-revolutionary class insult for an uppity lower-class person
terms.why_hard: The class sneer is the point (an ex-gentleman speaking); 'jerk' is too modern

terms.gloss: Threading dies (плашка) for 3/8-inch thread; Polesov's technical mania
terms.why_hard: плашка is a die for cutting threads, not a plate or tile; keep the imperial size

terms.gloss: Literally 'puff out your cheeks' — put on an important air; repeated twice on this page and later
terms.why_hard: Ostap means it literally as a stage direction, so keep the physical image rather than 'look important'

terms.gloss: Working capital; Ostap's businesslike term for cash to swindle
terms.why_hard: Use the standard accounting term in each language so the parody of business talk lands

terms.gloss: Soviet agitprop label 'backward person' (politically unenlightened), here used by Ostap as a joke
terms.why_hard: The Soviet cliché flavor should show; 'old-fashioned' is too mild

terms.gloss: Ostap's mock moral authorities: Count Leo Tolstoy (moralist) and Darwin
terms.why_hard: Keep 'Count' — the title is part of the sneer

proposed.zh: 托尔斯泰伯爵？还是达尔文？
proposed.ja: トルストイ伯爵か？ダーウィンか？

terms.term: На плохие шансы я не ловлю
terms.gloss: Odessa/gambler idiom: 'I don't bet on bad odds'
terms.why_hard: Ostap's card-sharp register; avoid a bland 'I don't take risks'

proposed.ja: 分の悪い賭けはしない主義でね

terms.gloss: Sunflower-seed husks: the parrot cracks seeds, the ubiquitous 1920s Russian snack
terms.why_hard: Not 'sunflower shells' in the botanical sense; sunflower seeds should be rendered the same way whenever they recur

conventions: Dialogue dashes: en uses double quotation marks with 'said' tags kept as in the Russian; zh uses “” ; ja uses 「」; never keep the Russian em-dash convention in the target text

proposed.en: fire inspector / the Gubpozhar (provincial fire department)
proposed.zh: 消防检查员 / 省消防局
proposed.ja: 消防検査官 / 州消防局

terms.gloss: children orphaned by the 1921-22 Volga famine, a stock phrase of Soviet charity
terms.why_hard: Ostap is reciting bureaucratic clichés; the reader must sense the famine without a paragraph of history

terms.gloss: stock propaganda phrase blaming social ills on tsarism
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a slogan being quoted, with the same wording every time it recurs in the book

proposed.en: the grim legacy of the tsarist regime

terms.term: Совместное воспитание обоих полов по комплексному методу
terms.gloss: 1920s progressive-pedagogy jargon (coeducation, the 'complex method' curriculum)
terms.why_hard: Must read as pompous educational jargon, not a plain description

proposed.en: coeducation of both sexes by the complex method
proposed.zh: 按综合教学法实行男女合校教育
proposed.ja: 総合教授法による男女共学

terms.gloss: 'whatever God has sent', i.e. a modest pot-luck meal; the narrator then lists a feast
terms.why_hard: The irony depends on echoing the phrase literally in the next sentence ('that day God sent...'), so use one rendering twice

terms.gloss: bison-grass flavoured vodka
terms.why_hard: Not generic vodka; the brand-like word recurs and should be transliterated with a short gloss

proposed.ja: ズブロッカ（バイソングラス入りウオッカ）

terms.gloss: forshmak, a chopped herring paste of Jewish/Odessa cuisine
terms.why_hard: Signals the Odessa-Jewish table; do not flatten to 'herring salad'

proposed.ja: ニシンのフォルシュマク

terms.gloss: side-whiskers in the style of Nicholas I, here on a woman
terms.why_hard: Reader must know it is a 19th-century male fashion; 'Nicholas I-style' carries it without a note

proposed.zh: 尼古拉一世式的半截鬓须
proposed.ja: ニコライ一世風の頬ひげ

terms.gloss: municipal/communal services, the department the almshouse falls under; Ostap toasts it
terms.why_hard: Bureaucratic term used as a toast; keep the officialese, not 'your household'

terms.gloss: Ostap's sneer at the almshouse as a 'kefir establishment' (a place of invalid diet)
terms.why_hard: Kefir must stay; it is the joke about old women fed on sour milk

terms.gloss: harmonium; vox humana is an organ/harmonium stop, which Ostap drops as showy Latin
terms.why_hard: Keep the Latin as Latin in all languages so Ostap's flourish stays a flourish

proposed.zh: 簧风琴 / vox humana（人声音栓）
proposed.ja: ハルモニウム / ヴォクス・フマーナ

terms.gloss: Gospel phrase 'let this cup pass from me' (Matt. 26:39), applied to the loudspeaker broadcast
terms.why_hard: Use the standard Bible wording of each target language so the allusion is recognised

proposed.en: that this cup might pass from them
proposed.ja: この杯が過ぎ去るように

conventions: Dialogue: replace Russian em-dash dialogue with target-language quotation marks (en “ ”, zh “ ”, ja 「」); keep narrator asides inside the same sentence rather than parenthesising them.
Soviet acronyms (губпожар, Доризул, etc.): transliterate once with a short parenthetical gloss on first occurrence in each language, then use the bare transliteration.
Japanese: no honorifics between Ostap and officials he is deceiving (plain names or 同志); use 同志 for товарищ in zh and ja, 'Comrade' in en.

terms.gloss: The former marshal of the nobility, Ostap's partner; narrator alternates name-patronymic and surname.
terms.why_hard: Spelling drift between transliteration systems and the two forms must both map to one fixed rendering per language.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 / 沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ / ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the 'great schemer' and driver of the plot.
terms.why_hard: Keep one transliteration; do not alternate Ostap/Bender unless the Russian does.

terms.gloss: Ostap's mock-tender signature on the note he leaves the widow; суслик = gopher/ground squirrel, a pet name.
terms.why_hard: It is a joke of self-belittling endearment, not a nickname used elsewhere; a literal 'ground squirrel' kills it, a random pet name loses the animal.

terms.gloss: Opening line of Fet's poem (1842), famous as a Varlamov romance; Ostap quotes it about the sleeping widow.
terms.why_hard: Reader must see it is a sung romance, not Ostap's own words; needs a rendering that reads as a quoted lyric, with a brief note.

proposed.en: 'Wake her not at break of day' (Fet's romance)
proposed.zh: “莫在黎明时将她唤醒”（费特的浪漫曲）
proposed.ja: 「暁に彼女を起こすな」（フェートのロマンス）

terms.gloss: Real small town in Voronezh province, chosen by Ostap as a plausibly dull business-trip destination.
terms.why_hard: Transliterate consistently; the humour is in its provincial obscurity, so no explanation beyond the name.

terms.gloss: NEP-era official term for the chronic shortage of consumer goods ('goods famine').
terms.why_hard: It is period jargon Ostap parrots deadpan; 'shortage' is flat, 'famine' must be kept as the mock-official phrase.

terms.gloss: Flowered English chintz, pre-revolutionary imported upholstery fabric now unobtainable.
terms.why_hard: Ситец is cheap printed cotton (chintz/calico), not silk or linen; the point is that even cheap cloth is precious under NEP.

terms.gloss: A vein on Ostap's forehead shaped like ижица (Ѵ), the last letter of the pre-1918 alphabet.
terms.why_hard: Untranslatable letter-shape joke; render as a V-shaped vein and name the letter only if the note budget allows.

proposed.en: a V-shaped vein, an izhitsa of the old alphabet
proposed.zh: 一条V字形的青筋，像旧字母表末尾的“伊日察”
proposed.ja: 旧字母のイジツァ（Ѵ）のようなV字形の静脈

terms.gloss: Narrator's recurring epithet for Ostap and Vorobyaninov, from Ostap's joke that the chair hunt is a 'concession' (NEP foreign-investor term).
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed word book-wide; 'partners' loses the NEP business parody.

terms.gloss: Second recurring narrator epithet for the pair, 'the partners'.
terms.why_hard: Keep distinct from концессионеры; the narrator rotates epithets deliberately.

terms.gloss: Money Ostap extorted from the Stargorod 'conspirators' of the Union of the Sword and Ploughshare, ostensibly 'for the children'.
terms.why_hard: Callback to the previous scene's cover story; keep the exact phrase so the reader recognises the swindle.

proposed.ja: 子供たちのための寄付金

terms.gloss: Horse-drawn cab and its driver, still the standard town transport in 1927.
terms.why_hard: 'Taxi' is anachronistic; 'cab' in en needs 'horse-cab' once so the reader does not picture a car.

terms.gloss: Cooperative Street in Stargorod, a typically renamed Soviet street.
terms.why_hard: Translate the meaning (it is a Soviet renaming joke), do not transliterate.

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the meddling, incompetent Stargorod mechanic and 'conspirator'.
terms.why_hard: Both forms must map to one rendering; the patronymic form is the narrator's mock-respectful usage.

proposed.zh: 波列索夫 / 维克托·米哈伊洛维奇
proposed.ja: ポレソフ / ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ

terms.gloss: Yard-keeper of an apartment building: sweeper, gatekeeper and semi-official watchman with police ties.
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' suggests indoor cleaning; the dvornik is a street authority figure, hence he can beat Polesov.

terms.gloss: Pereleshinsky Lane, the Stargorod street where Polesov lives and works.
terms.why_hard: Recurring address; fix one transliteration and one word for переулок (lane) book-wide.

terms.gloss: Polesov's cries while beaten: 'help!' and 'boor!', the latter a pre-revolutionary class insult (lower-class lout).
terms.why_hard: Хам carries old-regime contempt for the lower orders; a modern 'jerk' loses Polesov's absurd gentility.

terms.gloss: Gusishche, a low district of Stargorod that the railway crosses on an embankment.
terms.why_hard: A proper name, not 'goose-place'; transliterate consistently with earlier chapters.

terms.gloss: Alkhen (Alexander Yakovlevich), the 'shy thief' who runs the Stargorod old women's home and steals its property.
terms.why_hard: Diminutive nickname; keep as a name and let the earlier chapter's introduction carry it, no explanation here.

terms.gloss: Alkhen's freeloading relative who sells off the home's furniture; Ostap hails him familiarly as Pashka.
terms.why_hard: Diminutives Паша/Пашка must stay recognisably the same person as Паша Эмильевич.

proposed.zh: 帕沙·埃米利耶维奇 / 帕什卡
proposed.ja: パーシャ・エミーリエヴィチ / パーシカ

terms.gloss: The flea market / second-hand bazaar where stolen goods are sold.
terms.why_hard: Colloquial; needs an equally informal word, not 'market'.

terms.gloss: Tolstovka: a long belted blouse named after Tolstoy, standard 1920s Soviet clerk's wear.
terms.why_hard: Not a modern hoodie (толстовка today); the reader needs 'Tolstoy blouse' once.

proposed.ja: ネズミ色のトルストイ・シャツ

terms.gloss: Harmonium, the reed organ Alkhen's relatives carry off from the old women's home.
terms.why_hard: Not a piano or accordion; recurring prop in the Alkhen chapters.

terms.gloss: Ostap's catchphrase, 'The session continues!', parodying the chairman's formula after an interruption.
terms.why_hard: It recurs throughout the book and became a Russian proverb; it must be word-for-word identical every time.

terms.gloss: Ostap's familiar, condescending address to Vorobyaninov ('pops', 'old man').
terms.why_hard: Not literal 'father'; needs a fixed mock-affectionate vocative that works with Ostap's вы.

terms.gloss: The Moscow Furniture Museum where confiscated furniture, including some of the chairs, ended up.
terms.why_hard: A real early-Soviet institution; render plainly and consistently as a proper name.

terms.gloss: Chapter XIV title: the fake monarchist conspiracy Ostap invents; орало is archaic 'plough' (Isaiah's swords into ploughshares).
terms.why_hard: Орало must read as biblical-archaic, not as 'mouth' (орать); keep the sword/ploughshare inversion.

proposed.en: The Union of the Sword and Ploughshare

conventions: Dialogue: replace Russian dashes with double quotation marks in en, “” in zh, 「」 in ja; keep the narrator's dry asides unmarked, as in the Russian.

Ostap addresses Vorobyanov with вы plus familiar epithets (папаша): ja uses polite です/ます with ironic vocatives, no -さん/-様 on names except in mock-formal speech; zh uses 您 only where the Russian вы is pointedly formal.

Transliteration: en by a simplified BGN/PCGN (Vorobyaninov, Pereleshinsky), zh by the Xinhua Russian name table, ja by standard katakana with long vowels marked; Soviet renamed streets are translated by meaning, old names transliterated.

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk; the narrator almost always uses name + patronymic
terms.why_hard: Dropping the patronymic or switching between 'Vorobyaninov' and 'Ippolit Matveyevich' inconsistently loses the mock-ceremonial tone; each language needs one fixed transliteration

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Surname of the protagonist, used by the narrator when he is being an object of the plot rather than a person
terms.why_hard: Must match the transliteration system used for all other names (y vs i, single spelling in zh/ja)

terms.gloss: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova, Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law, dying on this page; the chapter title calls her 'мадам Петухова'
terms.why_hard: Same person appears as Клавдия Ивановна, старуха, мадам Петухова and покойная; renderings of the fixed name must stay identical

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
proposed.ja: クラヴディヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: The narrator's mock-respectful pre-revolutionary form of address for Klavdia Ivanovna (chapter 2 title 'Кончина мадам Петуховой')
terms.why_hard: 'Madame' is deliberately old-regime and ironic in 1927 Soviet Russia; 'Mrs.' or 太太 flattens the joke

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town ('Old Town'), Vorobyaninov's former home and site of his mansion; the chase begins there
terms.why_hard: It is an invented name that echoes 'старый город'; transliterate, do not translate, and keep one form across the book

terms.gloss: Furniture from the Gambs workshop, the St Petersburg maker of luxury furniture for the imperial court and nobility (19th c.); marks the chairs as valuable and identifiable
terms.why_hard: A careless reader sees a random adjective; the maker's name is a plot device (the chairs are later traced as Gambs chairs) and must be a recognisable proper name

terms.gloss: The dozen chairs of the drawing-room set; the twelve chairs of the title
terms.why_hard: Keep the count explicit and tie it to the title ('twelve'), while preserving that the old woman says 'a dozen' casually

terms.gloss: English chintz, the printed cotton upholstery of the chair set; the identifying detail Vorobyaninov and later the reader use to recognise the chairs
terms.why_hard: 'Calico' in en connotes plain cloth; the upholstery fabric here is glazed printed chintz, a pre-revolutionary luxury import

terms.gloss: Diamonds (the old-fashioned spelling брильянты, not бриллианты), the family jewels sewn into the chair seat
terms.why_hard: Old spelling is part of the period voice; in the target languages just be consistent (diamonds vs jewels vs stones) since the word recurs hundreds of times

terms.gloss: Records clerk of the ZAGS, the Soviet civil registry office (births, marriages, deaths); Vorobyaninov's humiliating post-revolutionary job
terms.why_hard: ZAGS is an acronym (запись актов гражданского состояния) no target reader knows; render the function, not the letters, and keep it as an epithet the narrator uses for him

terms.gloss: The search: the post-1917 requisition raid on the family's house when valuables were confiscated by the new authorities
terms.why_hard: Not a police search for evidence but a revolutionary confiscation; the reader needs 'that search' to land as a shared, understood historical event

terms.gloss: To squander an estate, literally 'let it go to the wind'; the mother-in-law's standing reproach
terms.why_hard: Must be an idiomatic 'squandered' in each language, not a literal wind image, and each language should use the same phrase whenever the reproach recurs

proposed.zh: 把我女儿的家产挥霍一空

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's sneering, stammered 'r-regalia' for the old woman's diamonds; 'regalia' is royal insignia, mocking her pretensions
terms.why_hard: The doubled consonant marks fury and contempt; a plain 'jewels' loses both the sarcasm and the sputter

proposed.ja: あなたの、れ、レガリアを

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's pince-nez with gold frame; his signature pre-revolutionary attribute throughout the book
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as 'glasses' loses a recurring visual emblem; needs one term everywhere (pince-nez / 夹鼻眼镜 / 鼻眼鏡)

terms.gloss: Colour of copper sulphate (vitriol): the blue-green pallor of the dying woman
terms.why_hard: Literal 'vitriolic' in English means acidic speech; the image is chemical blue-green, and the deadpan clinical tone is the joke

proposed.ja: 硫酸銅のような青緑色

terms.gloss: Daguerreotypes of high-ranking (сановный: holders of state rank) relatives on the mansion walls; shorthand for the lost gentry world
terms.why_hard: 'Dignitary' relatives means people with imperial civil-service ranks; 'important relatives' loses the tsarist rank system the book keeps invoking

proposed.ja: 高位の親族たちのダゲレオタイプ写真

terms.gloss: The agronomist's wife (colloquial feminine of агроном), a neighbour; the couple is 'чета агрономов'
terms.why_hard: The -ша suffix marks a wife by husband's profession, faintly comic and provincial; 'the agronomist' (female) misreads her, and zh/ja need the 'wife of' explicit

terms.gloss: The municipal public garden of a provincial town, with benches and evening couples; a fixed feature of Soviet provincial life in the book
terms.why_hard: Not a private garden or a 'city park' in the modern sense; a small tree-lined promenade ground

terms.gloss: Gypsy (Romani) choirs of the pre-revolutionary restaurant world, emblem of merchant-gentry debauchery Vorobyaninov dreams of
terms.why_hard: The reader needs the connotation of Moscow night-restaurant revelry, not folk music; consistent with later 'кутёж' scenes

terms.gloss: 'Amapa', a Brazilian maxixe-tango hit of the 1910s played by restaurant and ladies' orchestras; a period pop reference
terms.why_hard: A translator may treat it as a generic tango or invent a title; it is a real piece and should keep its name, perhaps with a short note

terms.gloss: A trotter (Orlov trotter), the fast carriage horse of rich pre-revolutionary Moscow; Vorobyaninov fantasises about his own
terms.why_hard: 'Racehorse' is wrong; it is a status carriage-horse, and the joke is the horse 'snorting contemptuously at pedestrians'

terms.gloss: Men's long underdrawers; Vorobyaninov's 'orange, ravishingly expensive' ones are a recurring comic object of desire
terms.why_hard: 'Underpants' or 'pants' misfires; the period item is long drawers, and the term must match its later reappearances

terms.gloss: The devotion of a lackey (liveried manservant); one of the gentry comforts Vorobyaninov dreams of recovering
terms.why_hard: 'Lackey' in en is now only figurative; the sense is a literal footman's servility, part of the old-regime fantasy

terms.gloss: Cannes, the French Riviera resort; emblem of the emigre-luxury Vorobyaninov hopes the diamonds will buy
terms.why_hard: Standard exonyms in each language; do not transliterate the Russian form

terms.gloss: 'The devil knows what': utter chaos, used of the state of Vorobyaninov's head
terms.why_hard: Recurs throughout the book in the narrator's deadpan register; pick one idiomatic equivalent per language and reuse it

conventions: Names: full name + patronymic wherever the Russian has it (Ippolit Matveyevich / 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 / イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ); one transliteration table for the whole book, Chinese using the standard 新华社 forms, Japanese katakana with long-vowel marks fixed once.
Dialogue: Russian dashes become double quotation marks in English, “” in Chinese, 「」 in Japanese; the narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the sentence, never moved to notes.

Address: вы between Vorobyaninov and his mother-in-law is rendered as formal register (Chinese 您, Japanese です/ます with さん-less name + patronymic); the narrator's ironic epithets (делопроизводитель загса, старуха) are kept as epithets, not replaced by names.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town where the first third of the novel is set (modelled on Odessa/Kremenchug-type towns).
terms.why_hard: Translating it literally ('Old Town') destroys the proper-name feel; it must be a fixed transliteration book-wide.

terms.gloss: The lane where house No. 7 (Polesov, the fortune-teller, the two front-firms) stands; recurs in the Stargorod chapters.
terms.why_hard: переулок is a lane/side-street, not a 'street' or 'alley'; spelling of the adjective must not drift between chapters.

terms.gloss: Second Empire (Napoleon III) architectural style, i.e. pompous 1860s eclecticism in a provincial imitation.
terms.why_hard: Not 'Second Reich'/Germany and not the Russian Empire; the joke is provincial pretension, so the term must be recognisable as the French style.

terms.gloss: Mikhail Artsybashev (1878-1927), author of the scandalous erotic novel 'Sanin'; here his lion-like bearded face is the punchline.
terms.why_hard: 'известного в свое время' is a jab at a forgotten celebrity; the reader needs a minimal gloss, and zh has an established form from Lu Xun's translations.

terms.gloss: Three words for the same lion faces in one paragraph, sliding from animal 'muzzles' to icon-painting 'countenances' to vulgar 'mugs'.
terms.why_hard: Flattening all three to 'faces' kills the deadpan register-shift; each language needs three distinct registers kept in this order.

proposed.zh: 兽脸 / 圣容 / 嘴脸
proposed.ja: 面（つら）／ 御尊顔 ／ 面相

terms.gloss: Keystones (замковые камни) at the top of window arches, where the lion heads are set.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'window keys' is nonsense; it is an architectural term.

terms.gloss: NEP-era producers' cooperative, the legal form under which small private business survived in the 1920s USSR; recurs throughout the book.
terms.why_hard: Not a 'company' or 'guild'; the word carries the specific flavour of legalised petty capitalism and should be one fixed rendering everywhere.

proposed.ja: アルテリ（労働組合式協同組合）

terms.gloss: Two near-identical ring breads: bublik (large, soft, Odessa/Ukrainian) and baranka (small, hard, Moscow); the sign's joke is that the artel passes one off as the other.
terms.why_hard: Rendering both as 'bagels'/'面包圈' erases the joke; keep two distinct names and a one-word gloss on first occurrence.

proposed.en: bubliki (Odessa ring rolls) / baranki (Moscow ring rolls)
proposed.zh: 布布利克（敖德萨大面包圈）/ 巴兰卡（莫斯科小面包圈）
proposed.ja: ブーブリク（オデッサ風リングパン）／バランカ（モスクワ風リングパン）

terms.gloss: Shop sign of the first front-firm at No. 7; a self-contradicting name (Odessa artel selling Moscow goods).
terms.why_hard: Sign text must be rendered as a sign (block layout, three lines), and the two bread words must match the glossary entries.

proposed.zh: 敖德萨布布利克劳动组合 —— 莫斯科巴兰卡
proposed.ja: オデッサ・ブーブリク・アルテリ ― モスクワ・バランカ

terms.gloss: Packing office 'Bystroupak' (portmanteau of быстрая упаковка, quick packing), the second front-firm at No. 7; parody of Soviet acronym-names.
terms.why_hard: A bare transliteration loses the parody; a translated portmanteau ('Quickpak') keeps the joke but must be used identically every time.

terms.gloss: 'Esteemed citizen-customers': Soviet commercial politesse that welds the revolutionary 'citizen' to the shopkeeper's 'customer'.
terms.why_hard: Dropping 'citizen' loses the parody of 1920s advertising Russian; keep the hyphenated compound.

proposed.ja: 敬愛なる市民顧客各位

terms.gloss: Illegally trading in textiles; спекуляция was a criminal offence, мануфактура means cloth/dry goods, not a factory.
terms.why_hard: 'Manufactory' or 'speculated in manufacturing' is a false friend; the sense is black-market cloth dealing.

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the locksmith-intellectual with the perpetually unassembled motorcycle; recurring Stargorod character.
terms.why_hard: Initials on a brass plate must match the full name used elsewhere; ja/zh need a fixed transcription of the surname.

terms.gloss: Tin sign on the fortune-teller's door, 'Fashions and Hats', a cover for her real trade.
terms.why_hard: Signage register: short, shop-sign phrasing, not a sentence; must read like a real shop sign in each language.

terms.gloss: Sparterie, stiffened esparto-and-buckram sheeting used as a hat-frame base in millinery.
terms.why_hard: Obscure even in Russian; a literal transliteration means nothing, so gloss it as hat-frame material.

proposed.ja: スパルトリー（帽子の芯地）

terms.gloss: 'Lone artisan': the official 1920s tax/legal category for a self-employed craftsman without hired labour; recurs (famously 'кустарь-одиночка с мотором').
terms.why_hard: It is a bureaucratic label, so it should sound like one; 'handicraftsman' loses the Soviet-form flavour.

terms.gloss: Rubber galoshes worn over shoes; new squeaky galoshes were a petty status item of the era.
terms.why_hard: Not 'boots' or 'rubber shoes'; the squeak of new galoshes is the comic detail and recurs later.

proposed.ja: オーバーシューズ（ガローシ）

terms.gloss: Arnold Böcklin's painting 'Isle of the Dead' (1880s), a reproduction hanging in every petty-bourgeois parlour of the period.
terms.why_hard: Reader must recognise a real painting and the cliché of owning it; use the standard title in each language.

terms.gloss: A 'fantaisie' frame: shop term for an ornamental fancy picture frame, borrowed French.
terms.why_hard: Not 'fantasy frame'; it is trade jargon for a decorative frame.

proposed.ja: 装飾額縁（ファンテジー額）

terms.gloss: Tablecloth in Richelieu cutwork embroidery, a fashionable petty-bourgeois household item.
terms.why_hard: Needs the embroidery term, not a person's name; 'Richelieu tablecloth' alone is opaque.

proposed.ja: リシュリュー刺繍のテーブルクロス

terms.gloss: The widow Gritsatsuyeva, a NEP-era shopkeeper's widow whom Bender will marry for her chair; major recurring character.
terms.why_hard: Her name and the epithet 'the widow' must be fixed; ja must decide between 未亡人 and katakana-only.

proposed.ja: 未亡人グリツァツーエワ

terms.gloss: The fortune-teller calls the middle-aged widow 'girl/young lady', flattering-professional address.
terms.why_hard: 'Girl' sounds rude in en; the tone is the oily politeness of a paid service.

terms.term: дама треф / червонная дама / трефовый король / бубновая дама
terms.gloss: Fortune-telling card figures: queen of clubs (dark/older woman), queen of hearts (fair/young), king of clubs, queen of diamonds; the widow insists on being the queen of hearts.
terms.why_hard: Suits must be translated consistently as playing-card terms, and the vanity joke (клубs vs hearts) depends on the reader knowing hearts is the flattering card.

proposed.en: queen of clubs / queen of hearts / king of clubs / queen of diamonds
proposed.zh: 梅花皇后 / 红心皇后 / 梅花国王 / 方块皇后
proposed.ja: クラブのクイーン／ハートのクイーン／クラブのキング／ダイヤのクイーン

terms.gloss: A 'séance': the fortune-teller's word for one paid card reading, pricing it like a spiritualist or cinema show.
terms.why_hard: 'Session' loses the mock-professional French borrowing; 'séance' in en suggests ghosts, so choose and keep one rendering.

chapter_titles.33: Глава X. Слесарь, попугай и гадалка

conventions: Signs, plates and inscriptions printed in block capitals in the Russian are set as separate lines in the same layout: en in CAPITALS, zh and ja as standalone centred lines without quotation marks.
Russian dash-dialogue becomes en double quotation marks, zh “ ” and ja 「 」; the narrator's deadpan asides stay in the same sentence, never moved to footnotes.

Personal names: en by simplified BGN/PCGN without diacritics (Gritsatsuyeva, Polesov), zh by Xinhua standard transcription tables, ja in katakana with ・ between name parts; patronymics and 'вдова/гражданин' epithets are kept, and ja adds no honorific suffix (-さん) that the Russian lacks.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility; the narrator calls him by name-and-patronymic throughout
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must be kept as a fixed two-part name, not cut to 'Ippolit' or swapped with the surname at random; zh/ja need one fixed transcription

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Surname of the same man; used when the narrator or Ostap is being formal or mocking
terms.why_hard: Reader must recognise it as the same person as Ippolit Matveyevich; transliteration must be stable (Vorobyaninov, not Vorobianinov/Vorobyaninoff)

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the 'great schemer', the con man; narrator alternates first name and surname
terms.why_hard: Keep both forms recognisable as one man; zh/ja have established renderings from prior translations that readers may know

proposed.ja: オスタップ / ベンデル

terms.gloss: Tikhon, Vorobyaninov's former yard-keeper in Stargorod, drunk in this scene
terms.why_hard: Simple name but must match wherever he appears; do not anglicise to 'Tikhon the janitor' inconsistently

terms.gloss: Ostap's mocking address: Vorobyaninov's cover story is that he is an emigre back from Paris; 'gospodin' is the pre-revolutionary 'Mister', already ironic in 1927
terms.why_hard: A translator who misses the earlier cover story renders it as a real Parisian; 'gospodin' should sound pointedly old-regime

proposed.ja: パリからお越しの旦那

terms.gloss: Diamonds (Madame Petukhova's jewels sewn into a chair); old-fashioned spelling 'brilyanty' rather than 'brillianty'
terms.why_hard: Chapter title 'Брильянтовый дым' and this page use the same word; keep one word ('diamonds', not 'brilliants'/'jewels' at random)

terms.gloss: Callback to Ostap's proverbial line from ch. 5 'may I also have the key to the apartment where the money is kept?' - i.e. 'anything else you'd like?'
terms.why_hard: Rendered literally it is nonsense; must echo the exact wording chosen for the ch. 5 line so the joke lands

proposed.en: And the key to the apartment?
proposed.zh: 还有放钱的那套房子的钥匙？
proposed.ja: それにアパートの鍵も？

terms.gloss: Colloquial/soldierly word for food, board, 'grub'
terms.why_hard: Ostap is talking like a hired hand negotiating board; a neutral 'food' loses the register

terms.gloss: NEP-era 'concession' (a licensed private enterprise, often foreign); Ostap's mock-official name for the treasure hunt, used book-wide
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed term in each language so the running joke ('the concession', 'the concessionaires') is recognisable; do not vary as 'venture/partnership/deal'

proposed.zh: 特许公司 / 合伙人 / 特许经营者
proposed.ja: コンセッション（利権事業） / 共同経営者 / 利権屋たち

terms.gloss: Ostap's catchphrase, now a Russian proverb: 'the ice has started moving' (things are under way) addressed to imaginary 'gentlemen of the jury'
terms.why_hard: Proverbial and repeated across the book; 'jury' must be the pre-revolutionary jury of the old courts, and the wording must never vary

proposed.en: The ice is moving, gentlemen of the jury!
proposed.zh: 冰河开动了，陪审员先生们！
proposed.ja: 氷が動き出したぞ、陪審員諸君！

terms.gloss: Pun on Vorobyaninov's old title 'district marshal of the nobility' (уездный предводитель дворянства) with 'Comanches' substituted
terms.why_hard: The joke depends on the reader knowing the fixed rendering of 'marshal of the nobility'; keep the same word for 'marshal/leader' and swap only 'nobility' for 'Comanches'

proposed.ja: コマンチ族の郡首席貴族

terms.gloss: Marshal of the nobility: elected head of the gentry of a district/province in Imperial Russia; Vorobyaninov's former post
terms.why_hard: Not a military marshal; needs a stable rendering the reader can attach to Vorobyaninov every time it recurs, including in puns

terms.gloss: Field marshal; Ostap 'promotes' Vorobyaninov to it as a mock apology
terms.why_hard: Should read as the highest Imperial military rank, contrasting with the civil 'marshal of the nobility' pun just before

terms.gloss: Military 'disposition' (battle order); mock-solemn word for the plan of action
terms.why_hard: A plain 'plan' loses the parodic military tone the narrator uses for the whole hunt

terms.gloss: Yard-keeper (dvornik): a live-in caretaker of a building who swept the yard, kept the gate and reported to the police; his basement lodge
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' or 'doorman' misses the yard and the semi-official role; must be one term wherever Tikhon appears

proposed.zh: 看院人 / 看院人的小屋

terms.gloss: Ostap parodies Soviet slogan style ('proletarian of mental labour', 'worker of the broom') to greet the drunk yard-keeper
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a mock poster slogan, not a genuine compliment; keep the capital-letter pomposity

proposed.en: A proletarian of mental labour! A worker of the broom!
proposed.zh: 脑力劳动的无产者！扫帚工作者！
proposed.ja: 知的労働のプロレタリアート！箒の労働者！

terms.gloss: Ostap's pet word, misusing 'congenial' (properly 'of kindred genius') to mean 'brilliant'
terms.why_hard: It is a recurring verbal tic; pick one slightly-off word and keep it every time, rather than a correct 'brilliant'

terms.gloss: 'Poshlost': vulgar, petty, banal-minded; Ostap's favourite insult
terms.why_hard: No single English word; 'vulgar' alone is too coarse, 'banal' too weak. Fix one rendering per language and reuse it

terms.gloss: Opening line of a well-known late-19th-century urban ballad ('There were merry days, I lived it up'), bawled by drunk Tikhon with stuttered 'Byvyvyvali'
terms.why_hard: Should be recognisable as a song title, with the drunken stutter reproduced; a translator may need a short note that it is a popular drinking song

proposed.zh: 曾、曾、曾有过快活的日子……
proposed.ja: た、た、楽しい日々があった……

terms.gloss: Cheap wall clock with a pendulum and a cylindrical weight on a chain, standard in poor households
terms.why_hard: The brass weight Tikhon bangs his head on is the point; 'clock' alone leaves the image unclear

terms.gloss: Peaked cloth cap worn by tradesmen and yard-keepers
terms.why_hard: Not a military cap; 'cap' is fine but keep it consistent with other characters' hats

terms.gloss: A red-and-black checked flannel 'cowboy' shirt, a 1920s fashion item; Ostap's only shirt
terms.why_hard: The quotation marks show it is a trade name; keep 'cowboy shirt' rather than a generic 'checked shirt'

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's 'moon-coloured waistcoat', a recurring epithet from ch. 1 ('known to the reader')
terms.why_hard: The narrator relies on the reader remembering the earlier description; the epithet must be word-for-word the same as in ch. 1

proposed.en: the moonlight waistcoat already known to the reader
proposed.zh: 读者已经熟悉的那件月光色背心
proposed.ja: 読者ご存じの月光色のチョッキ

terms.gloss: Made of garus, a coarse worsted wool yarn; here a bright-blue knitted waistcoat
terms.why_hard: Obscure fabric word; render as 'wool/worsted' and not leave transliterated

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash dialogue becomes double quotation marks in en, “” in zh, and 「」 in ja; keep one exchange per paragraph as in the original.
Address: Ostap and Vorobyaninov say вы to each other; Vorobyaninov says ты to Tikhon. Mark this in ja by plain form + お前/君 for ты versus polite form for вы, and in zh by 您 for вы; en uses tone only.

Names: one fixed transliteration table for the whole book (Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, Ostap Bender, Tikhon); the narrator's alternation between first-name-patronymic and surname is preserved, never normalised.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Chapter III title; an old Russian lubok print / edifying-tract title, 'The Mirror of the Sinner', showing the sinner's soul and death
terms.why_hard: Archaic Church-Slavonic 'зерцало' must sound old and pious, not modern 'mirror'; the mock-solemn framing of Father Fyodor's greed is the joke

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the greedy provincial priest, third treasure-hunter of the novel; also 'отец Востриков', 'батюшка', 'Федя', 'Федор Иваныч'
terms.why_hard: The narrator switches among four forms of his name for comic register; each must map to one stable set per language

proposed.zh: 费奥多尔·沃斯特里科夫神父
proposed.ja: フョードル・ヴォストリコフ神父

terms.gloss: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova, Vorobyaninov's dying mother-in-law who confesses the jewels' hiding place
terms.why_hard: Name-plus-patronymic must be kept whole and transliterated identically on every page

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, former marshal of the nobility, main treasure-hunter
terms.why_hard: Long surname needs one fixed spelling; zh/ja syllable division varies between translators

terms.gloss: Church of Sts Florus and Laurus (folk form Frol and Lavr), patron saints of horses; Fr Fyodor's parish
terms.why_hard: Latinising to 'Florus and Laurus' loses the rustic folk form; leaving 'Frol and Lavr' needs no note if 'Saints' is implied by context

proposed.en: the Church of Frol and Lavr

terms.gloss: Honorific for a priest's wife (here Katerina Alexandrovna); also 'попадья' in the narrator's plainer register
terms.why_hard: 'Little mother' is a mistranslation; it is a title of the priest's wife, not the priest's mother; матушка/попадья should be distinguished only by tone

proposed.ja: 神父の妻（マートゥシカ）

terms.gloss: Affectionate-respectful word for a parish priest, used by the narrator with mock deference
terms.why_hard: Not 'little father'; it is simply how one refers to a priest, and the irony is in the narrator's use of it

terms.gloss: Car of the uispolkom (uyezd executive committee, the local Soviet government), bearing state licence plate No. 1
terms.why_hard: The acronym must be unpacked without a footnote; 'Гос. № 1' is a licence plate, not a car model

proposed.en: the District Executive Committee car, state plate No. 1
proposed.zh: 县执行委员会的汽车，公务牌照1号
proposed.ja: 郡執行委員会の自動車、官用ナンバー1号

terms.gloss: 'Infernal machine' – period term for a time bomb, here applied to the smoky car
terms.why_hard: Translate the idiom literally so the bomb joke survives; 'hellish contraption' loses the fixed phrase

terms.gloss: Borrowed stock-exchange word (agiotage, speculative frenzy) used for the priest's excitement
terms.why_hard: The comic point is the financial metaphor for a priest's greed; flat 'excitement' loses it

proposed.en: in a state of complete agiotage
proposed.zh: 处于极度亢奋（投机热）之中
proposed.ja: すっかり投機熱にとりつかれた状態で

terms.gloss: All-Night Vigil, the Orthodox Saturday-evening and pre-feast service
terms.why_hard: Not literally all night; use the established Orthodox term in each language

terms.gloss: Priest's cassock (here a warm quilted one)
terms.why_hard: Should not become 'robe' or 'gown'; Orthodox clerical term recurs whenever Fr Fyodor is described

terms.gloss: The hymn to the Theotokos 'It Is Truly Meet' (Axion Estin) that Fr Fyodor hums to himself
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered by the liturgical title used by Orthodox churches in each language, not translated word-for-word

proposed.ja: 「まことに当然なり」（生神女讃詞）

terms.gloss: Two tiers of pre-revolutionary church schooling: junior ecclesiastical school, then seminary
terms.why_hard: Both are often flattened to 'seminary'; the passage tracks his career step by step

proposed.zh: 教会初级学校 / 神学院

terms.term: рукоположен в диаконы … посвящен в сан священника
terms.gloss: Ordination as deacon, then as priest; 'сан' = clerical rank, also 'почтенный сан'
terms.why_hard: Keep the two-step ordination and render 'сан' as rank/dignity consistently across the book

proposed.en: ordained deacon … ordained to the priesthood
proposed.zh: 被授予辅祭职 … 被授予司祭圣职
proposed.ja: 輔祭に叙聖され … 司祭の位に叙された

terms.gloss: The unnamed 'district town of N' (Stargorod), a Gogolian convention for provincial anywhere
terms.why_hard: Keep the letter N and the literary convention; 'уездный' is the pre-1929 district unit

terms.gloss: Church-flavoured word for an acquisitive, grasping man (from the medieval 'non-possessors' controversy)
terms.why_hard: Plain 'greedy' loses the ecclesiastical solemnity of the narrator's verdict

terms.gloss: Fr Fyodor's dream of his own candle factory in Samara; a running motif of the whole novel
terms.why_hard: Recurs as a proverb-like refrain; must use exactly the same words everywhere

proposed.en: his own little candle factory in Samara
proposed.zh: 在萨马拉的自家小蜡烛厂
proposed.ja: サマーラの自分のロウソク工場

terms.gloss: Fixed and working capital, mock-economic jargon for a priest's scheming
terms.why_hard: Use the standard accounting terms so the parody of business prose reads as such

terms.gloss: Soap from the state 'Plough and Hammer' (Плуг и молот) factory, a real Soviet brand of the 1920s
terms.why_hard: The adjective hides a factory name; rendering as a brand keeps the joke that the priest's soap costs three times the state product

terms.gloss: Pood, old Russian weight of about 16.4 kg
terms.why_hard: Convert or keep consistently; 'наваривал его пуды' is hyperbole, not an exact quantity

terms.gloss: Townsfolk, with the 1920s pejorative tinge of petty-bourgeois philistines
terms.why_hard: Neutral 'inhabitants' drops the sneer; 'philistines' overdoes it

terms.gloss: Pozharsky cutlets, breaded minced-chicken cutlets famous from Pushkin's Torzhok verse
terms.why_hard: A named dish, not 'fireman's cutlets'; keep proper name and the point that rabbit is passed off as chicken

proposed.ja: ポジャルスキー・カツレツ

terms.gloss: Soviet 'ration' (food allowance), here 'кроличий паек' applied to the family's rabbit diet
terms.why_hard: The Soviet rationing word is the joke; 'diet' alone loses the period flavour

terms.gloss: The Vostrikovs' dog, frightened away by the rabbits
terms.why_hard: Pet name to transliterate once and reuse

conventions: Names: keep name + patronymic; en uses Fyodor/Katerina/Ippolit spellings (no diacritics); zh uses standard 新华社 transliteration with ·; ja uses katakana with long vowels and no added honorifics beyond 神父
Orthodox clerical vocabulary (матушка, батюшка, ряса, всенощная, сан) is rendered with the Orthodox-specific term of each target language, never with Catholic or Protestant equivalents
Dialogue dashes become en “…” quotes, zh “…” quotes, ja 「…」; the narrator's dry mock-solemn asides are kept as full sentences, never softened or footnoted
